The quality manager responds: "We did an FMEA on the launch process and used the results to define controls." Is this an adequate response to the Clause 6 requirement?
D is correct. ISO 9001:2015 Clause 6 requires organizations to determine risks and opportunities and take appropriate actions — but does NOT prescribe how. FMEA, SWOT analysis, risk registers, brainstorming sessions, process hazard analyses — all are acceptable methods depending on the context. ISO 9001:2015 explicitly states it does not require formal risk management per ISO 31000. The standard requires proportionate risk thinking, not a specific methodology. An FMEA for a product launch process is entirely appropriate and demonstrates systematic risk identification and control planning — exactly what Clause 6 intends.
§III · Topic 7
Quality Gurus

The exam tests knowledge of the major quality thinkers and their specific, distinctive contributions. The key is associating each guru with their unique concept — not just knowing they were "important to quality." The exam distinguishes between gurus with similar ideas.

📚 BoK: III.E.2
⚠️ Trap risk: High — Deming vs. Juran attributions; Crosby's "zero defects" vs. Deming's variation reduction
1
The Six Major Quality Gurus — Quick Reference
GuruUnique contributionKey concept/toolFamous for
W. Edwards DemingSystem of Profound Knowledge; 14 Points of Management; variation reduction through statistical methodsPDCA/PDSA cycle; SPC; 14 Points; drive out fearJapan's quality transformation; 85-94% of problems are system problems; common vs. special cause variation
Joseph M. JuranQuality Trilogy (Planning, Control, Improvement); vital few/useful many (Pareto principle); cost of qualityQuality trilogy; Pareto analysis; quality planning road mapMeasuring quality in dollars (COQ); quality must be managed like finance; internal customer concept
Philip B. CrosbyZero Defects philosophy; "quality is free" (non-conformance costs money); quality measured by cost of non-conformanceZero Defects; Cost of Poor Quality (COPQ); 14-step quality improvement process"Quality is conformance to requirements" — not goodness; prevention not appraisal; zero defects as a goal
Armand V. FeigenbaumTotal Quality Control (TQC) — quality is everyone's responsibility, not just the quality department'sTotal Quality Control; hidden quality factory conceptFirst to identify that the true cost of quality was hidden; quality is a business strategy not just a technical function
Kaoru IshikawaQuality circles; cause-and-effect (fishbone/Ishikawa) diagram; Company-Wide Quality Control (CWQC)Ishikawa/fishbone diagram; quality circles; seven basic quality toolsWorker participation in quality; made quality tools accessible to front-line workers; quality for all employees
Walter A. ShewhartFather of statistical quality control; invented the control chart; original PDCA (as PDSA)Control charts; statistical process control; PDSA cycleDistinguishing common cause from special cause variation; basis for all modern SPC
2
The Critical Distinctions the Exam Tests
⚠️ Deming vs. Juran — most confused pairing
Deming: Most quality problems are system problems (85-94%) — management must change the system. Focus on statistical methods and reducing variation. Drive out fear. No numerical goals without methods.

Juran: Quality must be managed like finance — measured in dollars (COQ). Vital few causes produce most defects (Pareto). Quality trilogy: Plan → Control → Improve. Both are systems thinkers but with different primary lenses.
⚠️ Crosby vs. everyone else on "zero defects"
Crosby's zero defects: A performance standard — employees should do their job right the first time. Motivational goal. Quality = conformance to requirements.

Deming's view: Zero defects as a slogan without methods is harmful. You cannot wish variation away. Reducing variation requires understanding the system and applying statistical methods — not exhortations to work harder.

The exam will present a scenario with slogans without methods (posters, pep talks, zero defect campaigns) and ask which guru's philosophy this approach violates — the answer is Deming.
3
Deming's 14 Points — Key Points to Know

The exam tests recognition of Deming's key points — you don't need all 14 but should know the most frequently tested:

PointCore messageQuality management implication
Drive out fearPeople must feel safe to speak up about quality problemsPsychological safety is a prerequisite for quality culture
Cease dependence on inspectionBuild quality in; don't inspect it inPrevention over appraisal as the primary quality strategy
End the practice of awarding business on price aloneTotal cost of ownership > unit priceSupplier quality, reliability, and partnership matter more than lowest bid
Eliminate work standards/quotasNumerical targets without methods are counterproductiveSetting targets without improving the system produces workarounds, not improvement
Institute leadershipSupervisors should help people do better work, not police complianceManagement's job is system improvement, not fault-finding
4
Juran's Quality Trilogy
PhaseWhat it involvesAnalogy to financial management
Quality PlanningIdentifying customers, determining their needs, developing products/processes that meet those needsBudgeting — establishing the plan for quality
Quality ControlEvaluating actual performance, comparing to goals, acting on the differenceCost control — maintaining the quality plan
Quality ImprovementEstablishing infrastructure for improvement, identifying projects, establishing teams, providing resourcesCapital investment — raising quality performance above current levels
💡 Why Juran uses financial analogies
Juran believed quality must be managed as a financial discipline — because that is the language senior management understands. By structuring quality management like financial management (planning, control, improvement), Juran made quality a business management responsibility, not just a technical function.
5
Practice Questions
An organization launches a quality improvement initiative with banners reading "Zero Defects!", employee pledges to work error-free, and manager speeches exhorting people to "care more about quality." Six months later, defect rates are unchanged. Which quality guru's philosophy most precisely predicts this outcome — and why?
C is correct. Deming's 14 Points include: "Eliminate slogans, exhortations, and targets for the workforce asking for zero defects and new levels of productivity. Such exhortations only create adversarial relationships, as the bulk of the causes of low quality and low productivity belong to the system and thus lie beyond the power of the workforce." The organization is treating a system problem (defects produced by process variation, design, equipment, materials) as an attitude problem. Changing attitudes without changing the system produces no quality improvement — exactly what happened.
5
Deming's 14 Points — Complete List

All 14 Points appear in the handbook. The exam tests recognition and application — here are all 14 with quality management context:

#PointQuality management implication
1Create constancy of purpose for improvement of product and serviceQuality improvement is not a project — it is a permanent organizational commitment
2Adopt the new philosophyWestern management must awaken to the quality challenge; accept zero tolerance for mistakes and poor workmanship
3Cease dependence on inspection to achieve qualityBuild quality into the product; don't inspect it in — prevention over detection
4End the practice of awarding business on price aloneTotal cost of ownership; supplier quality matters; single-source partnerships over multiple bidders
5Improve constantly and forever the system of production and serviceContinuous improvement is never-ending; every process can always be improved
6Institute training on the jobWorkers cannot do good work if they don't know how; training is a management responsibility, not an optional extra
7Institute leadershipThe job of supervisors is to help people do better work, not to police compliance; supervision = coaching
8Drive out fearPeople must feel safe to report quality problems, admit errors, and suggest improvements without fear of punishment
9Break down barriers between staff areasQuality problems occur at departmental interfaces; silos prevent quality improvement; cross-functional teamwork is required
10Eliminate slogans, exhortations, and targetsQuality posters and pep talks without methods only create frustration; problems are in the system, not in worker attitude
11Eliminate work standards and numerical quotasProduction quotas without quality constraints drive out quality; quantity targets without method support are counterproductive
12Remove barriers to pride of workmanshipAnnual performance reviews, merit ratings, and management by objective destroy teamwork and quality; people want to do good work
13Institute a vigorous program of education and self-improvementContinuous learning for everyone — not just technical skills; organizational learning capability is a competitive advantage
14Put everyone in the company to work to accomplish the transformationQuality transformation requires total involvement — from top management to every employee; quality is everyone's responsibility
⚠️ The 3 most tested Deming Points on the CMQ/OE exam
Point 3 (Cease dependence on inspection): The scenario — "We're adding more inspectors to solve our quality problem." Deming's response: inspection finds defects but doesn't prevent them; build quality into the process.

Point 8 (Drive out fear): The scenario — "Workers don't report near-misses because they fear discipline." This is Point 8 — fear culture prevents quality information from flowing. Quality culture requires psychological safety.

Point 10 (Eliminate slogans): The scenario — "Zero Defects Day" campaign with posters, speeches, and worker pledges but no process changes. Deming explicitly opposed this — problems are in systems, not in attitudes.
6
Juran's Quality Planning Road Map

Within Juran's Quality Trilogy, Quality Planning has a specific structured process called the Quality Planning Road Map:

StepActivity
1Identify the customers (both internal and external)
2Determine the needs of those customers
3Translate those needs into our language (technical specifications)
4Develop a product that can respond to those needs
5Optimize the product features so as to meet our needs as well as customer needs
6Develop a process that is able to produce the product
7Optimize the process
8Prove that the process can produce the product under operating conditions
9Transfer the process to Operations
💡 Juran's Quality Planning Road Map connects to QFD
Steps 1-3 of the Road Map are exactly what QFD does — identifying customers, determining needs, and translating them into technical language (the House of Quality translates VOC into engineering specifications). Juran provided the strategic framework; QFD provides the operational tool.
7
Additional Practice Questions
A plant manager announces a "Quality Awareness Month" with banners, speeches, and an employee pledge to achieve zero defects. She tells the quality director: "Deming would approve — we're demonstrating management commitment to quality." Is she correct?
A is correct. Deming's Point 10 is one of his most important and most misunderstood: "Eliminate slogans, exhortations, and targets for the workforce asking for zero defects and new levels of productivity. Such exhortations only create adversarial relationships, as the bulk of the causes of low quality and low productivity belong to the system and thus lie beyond the power of the workforce." The plant manager has the right instinct (management commitment is important) but the wrong method (slogans and pledges are exactly what Deming said NOT to do). Genuine management commitment means investing in system improvement: process redesign, equipment maintenance, training, measurement systems — not motivational campaigns.
📚 Additional Reference: Gryna, Chua & Defeo, Juran's Quality Planning and Analysis
Written by Juran's direct collaborators, this is the primary source for the complete Juran methodology. Key additions: the 9-step Quality Planning Road Map with full worked industry examples; the most comprehensive COQ treatment available (how to conduct a COQ study and present to management); the Juran improvement methodology connecting directly to DMAIC. Strongly recommended for §III questions on quality planning, COQ, and quality philosophies.
✦
From Juran — Fitness for Use & the Quality Spiral

Source: Juran, J.M., Juran on Quality by Design, Free Press/McGraw-Hill, 1992

Juran's primary contribution to quality philosophy is reframing quality as customer-defined fitness for use — not conformance to internal specifications. Two foundational concepts:

ConceptDefinitionQuality management implication
Fitness for UseQuality means a product performs its intended purpose under the conditions of use the customer will actually experienceSpecifications that meet internal standards but not customer use conditions are not quality; customer VOC must drive specification design, not internal engineering convenience
Quality CharacteristicsJuran identifies: Technological (hardness, voltage), Psychological (taste, beauty), Time-oriented (reliability, maintainability), Contractual (warranty provisions), Ethical (courtesy, honesty)Quality is multi-dimensional; a product can have excellent technological characteristics but fail on ethical or time-oriented dimensions — all must be managed
The Quality SpiralQuality flows through interconnected organizational functions: market research → product development → design → purchasing → manufacturing → process control → inspection → sales → customer service → back to market researchQuality problems at any point in the spiral propagate to subsequent stages; the spiral concept precedes and underpins process-based quality management (ISO 9001's process approach)
💡 Juran vs. Crosby on "conformance"
Crosby defined quality as "conformance to requirements" — meeting specifications. Juran defined quality as "fitness for use" — meeting customer needs. These produce different organizational behaviors:

Conformance to requirements (Crosby): If the spec says ±0.05mm and we hit ±0.05mm, quality is achieved — regardless of whether the customer's product actually works in use.

Fitness for use (Juran): The real test is whether the product performs its intended function for the customer. A product can conform to specifications and still fail fitness for use if the specifications were wrong.

The CMQ/OE exam tests both definitions — know which philosopher said what and what each implies for quality practice.
A pharmaceutical company's product meets all internal specifications and passes all internal quality tests. However, customers report the tablets are too large to swallow comfortably. The quality director says "our product meets all specs — this is not a quality issue." A quality consultant disagrees. Which quality philosophy does the consultant apply?
A is correct. This is the classic Juran fitness for use scenario: the product conforms to internal specifications but fails the customer's real need (easy swallowability is a quality characteristic Juran would classify as psychological and time-oriented). The quality director's response reflects Crosby's conformance-to-requirements definition. The consultant's disagreement reflects Juran's fitness for use: if the specifications didn't include tablet size parameters that ensure comfortable swallowability, the specifications are incomplete — not the customer's expectation. Juran's response: go back to market research in the quality spiral to understand the customer's actual use conditions and redesign the specification accordingly.
§III · Topic 8
Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA)

CAPA is the quality management system's primary mechanism for eliminating problems and preventing their recurrence. The exam tests the distinction between correction, corrective action, and preventive action — three different responses at three different time horizons.

📚 BoK: III.D
⚠️ Key trap: Corrective action addresses ROOT CAUSE — not just the symptom
1
Three Levels of Response
Response typeWhat it addressesTimingExample
Correction (containment)The immediate nonconformance — fix or contain the specific problem that occurredImmediate — right nowQuarantine the nonconforming batch; rework the defective parts; sort 100% of suspect inventory
Corrective actionThe ROOT CAUSE of the nonconformance — eliminate what caused it so it cannot recurShort-medium term — after root cause analysisIdentify that the batch failure was caused by a supplier material change not communicated; update supplier specification change notification procedure
Preventive actionA POTENTIAL nonconformance — eliminate the risk before any failure occursProactive — before problems occurReviewing the specification change notification procedure for all critical suppliers BEFORE a failure occurs; updating procedures based on near-miss analysis
⚠️ The most common CAPA failure — retraining as "corrective action"
The exam will present a nonconformance followed by this corrective action: "Operator retrained on procedure." This is NOT corrective action — it is correction at best. Why? Because it assumes the root cause is operator knowledge without verifying it through root cause analysis. If the actual root cause is a procedure ambiguity, process design flaw, or measurement problem, retraining does nothing. Real corrective action requires: (1) verified root cause analysis, (2) action that eliminates that specific root cause, (3) verification that the action was effective.
2
The CAPA Process
StepActivityKey output
1Identify and document the nonconformance or near-missProblem statement with data
2Immediate containment — prevent further impactQuarantine, sort, rework, or stop production
3Root cause analysis — verified, not assumedConfirmed root cause(s)
4Develop corrective action plan — addresses root causeAction plan with owners and dates
5Implement corrective actionsSystem/process/procedure changes
6Verify effectiveness — confirm the problem is resolvedData showing recurrence rate after CA implementation
7Close CAPA — document and close when effectiveness is confirmedClosed CAPA record
💡 Verification of effectiveness is mandatory
The CAPA process is not complete when the corrective action is implemented — it is complete only when there is DATA showing the root cause has been eliminated and the problem has not recurred. Many organizations close CAPAs at implementation, then discover the same problem recurring. Effectiveness verification is the step that makes CAPA genuinely preventive.
3
Practice Questions
A customer returns 200 units with a dimensional failure. The quality team: (1) quarantines all suspect inventory and issues a recall of shipped units, (2) conducts an RCA finding that a worn tooling die exceeded its replacement schedule, (3) replaces the die and updates the tooling replacement schedule and monitoring system, (4) monitors production for 60 days with zero recurrence, then closes the CAPA. Which statement correctly describes the CAPA process followed?
C is correct. This follows the complete CAPA process: (1) Containment — quarantine and recall address immediate impact. (2) Root cause analysis — verified that a worn die was the cause (not assumed). (3) Corrective action — replacing the die (fixing current cause) AND updating the replacement schedule and monitoring system (addressing the systemic gap that allowed the die to wear beyond limits). (4) Effectiveness verification — 60-day monitoring with zero recurrence confirms the root cause was eliminated. (5) Closure — completed after effectiveness is confirmed, not after implementation. This is the model CAPA process.
4
Root Cause Analysis Methods

Root cause analysis is the engine of effective CAPA. The exam tests which RCA method is most appropriate for different types of quality problems:

RCA MethodBest forHow it works
5 WhysSimple, linear cause-effect chains. Quick problems with single root cause.Ask "Why?" sequentially; each answer becomes the next "Why?" question; stop when you reach an actionable root cause (typically 4-6 iterations)
Fishbone / Ishikawa DiagramComplex problems with multiple potential cause categories. Brainstorming all possible causes before investigating.Identify all potential causes organized by 6M categories (Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature); fishbone generates hypotheses — data collection verifies which are actual causes
Fault Tree Analysis (FTA)Safety-critical systems; reliability engineering; complex systems with multiple failure paths that combine to cause a top-level event.Top-down: start with the undesired event (top) and work downward through AND/OR gates to identify the combinations of basic events that can cause it
Kepner-Tregoe (KT) AnalysisDistinguishing between "IS" and "IS NOT" to narrow the cause space. Especially effective for complex problems where the cause is not obvious.Define the problem (IS: what, where, when, to what extent). Define what IS NOT but could be. The cause must explain all IS observations AND explain why the IS NOTs don't have the problem. Systematically eliminates causes that don't fit the full IS/IS NOT pattern.
Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)Proactive RCA — identifying potential failure modes BEFORE they occurSystematic examination of what could fail in a system, the effects of each failure, and the causes; uses RPN to prioritize prevention actions
💡 Kepner-Tregoe IS/IS NOT — the exam's most tested advanced RCA method
The Kepner-Tregoe method is specifically designed to find the root cause by systematically narrowing down based on what IS and IS NOT affected. Example:

Problem: Dimensional failures on Part X
IS: Machine 3, Shift 2, Aluminum material, since Monday
IS NOT: Machine 1 or 2, Shift 1 or 3, Steel material, before Monday

The root cause MUST explain why Machine 3/Shift 2/Aluminum/after Monday has failures AND why Machine 1, 2, Shift 1, 3, Steel, before Monday do NOT. This systematically eliminates causes that fit only part of the pattern. In this case, "Machine 3 tooling was changed on Monday Shift 2 specifically for aluminum parts" would explain the full IS/IS NOT pattern — machine-only or material-only causes would fail the IS NOT test.
5
CAPA vs. Correction — Complete Distinction Table
CorrectionCorrective ActionPreventive Action
TriggerA nonconformance HAS occurredA nonconformance HAS occurredA potential nonconformance has been identified — but has NOT occurred
TargetThe specific nonconforming item/batchThe ROOT CAUSE that produced the nonconformanceThe RISK that could produce a future nonconformance
GoalFix or contain THIS occurrencePrevent RECURRENCE of this type of problemPrevent OCCURRENCE of a problem that hasn't happened yet
ISO 9001 termCorrection (also: containment, disposition)Corrective action (requires RCA)Risk-based thinking / opportunity (ISO 9001:2015 replaced formal PA requirement with risk management)
ExampleSort and rework the 500 nonconforming unitsFind and fix the worn tooling die that caused the nonconformance; update replacement scheduleReview all tooling dies across all lines to identify any approaching wear limits before failure
6
Additional Practice Questions
A quality team is investigating a dimensional defect that appears on Product A but NOT on Product B (same material), on Machine 2 but NOT Machine 1 (same setup), only during the afternoon shift, and only since the new operator joined 3 weeks ago. Which RCA method is best suited to exploit this IS/IS NOT pattern systematically?
D is correct. Kepner-Tregoe analysis is specifically designed for exactly this situation: multiple IS/IS NOT observations that narrow the cause space. The root cause must explain: WHY Product A (not B), WHY Machine 2 (not Machine 1), WHY afternoon (not morning), WHY only since 3 weeks ago. A cause like "the new afternoon operator uses a different measurement technique on Machine 2 for Product A" would explain the full IS/IS NOT pattern. 5 Whys (A) is too linear for multi-variable IS/IS NOT analysis. Fishbone (B) generates potential causes but doesn't systematically use the IS/IS NOT boundaries to eliminate them. FTA (D) works top-down for complex safety systems, not for operational IS/IS NOT problem-solving.
A quality manager receives a CAPA from a supplier for nonconforming seal dimensions. The supplier's CAPA states: "Root cause: Operator error. Corrective action: Operator warned and retrained on seal dimension inspection." What is wrong with this CAPA response, and what should the quality manager require instead?
D is correct. "Operator error" is one of the most common shallow root cause statements — it describes WHO made the error without asking WHY they made it. A complete RCA would ask: Why did the operator error? → The inspection procedure tolerance call-out was ambiguous. Why was it ambiguous? → The work instruction was updated 6 months ago but the tolerance tables were not revised to match. → ROOT CAUSE: Document control process failure that allowed work instructions and tolerance tables to diverge. Corrective action: fix the work instruction, update the document control procedure to prevent future divergence, and verify effectiveness by checking for similar divergences in other work instructions. Retraining the operator on the ambiguous procedure would not prevent the next operator from making the same error.
§III · Topic 9
Risk Management

Quality managers must identify, assess, and respond to risks that could compromise quality outcomes. The exam tests the risk management process, risk prioritization using probability × impact, and the four risk response strategies.

📚 BoK: III.C / III.E
1
The Risk Management Process
StepActivityOutput
1. IdentifySystematically identify all potential risks — internal and external — that could affect quality outcomesRisk register (list of identified risks)
2. Analyze/AssessEvaluate each risk for: Probability (likelihood of occurring) and Impact (consequence if it occurs)Risk priority scores; risk matrix
3. PrioritizeRank risks by priority — typically Probability × Impact scorePrioritized risk list for action planning
4. RespondDevelop response strategies for high-priority risksRisk response plans with owners
5. MonitorTrack identified risks; watch for new risks; review effectiveness of responsesUpdated risk register; risk review meetings
2
The Four Risk Response Strategies
StrategyWhat it meansWhen to useExample
AvoidEliminate the risk by changing the plan — don't do the activity that creates the riskRisk probability or impact is very high and unacceptable; alternative approach existsDon't use the risky new supplier; use a qualified alternative
MitigateReduce the probability or impact of the risk — make it smaller or less likelyRisk cannot be avoided but can be reduced to acceptable levelsAdd incoming inspection for a supplier with variable quality; implement early warning metrics
TransferShift the risk and its consequences to another party — insurance, warranties, contractsRisk is financial in nature; another party can bear it more efficientlyRequire supplier quality warranty; purchase product liability insurance
AcceptAcknowledge the risk and choose to live with it — with or without a contingency planRisk probability or impact is low; cost of mitigation exceeds potential lossAccept minor delay risk on non-critical path; maintain contingency budget for minor overruns
💡 Active vs. Passive Acceptance
Active acceptance: acknowledging the risk and creating a contingency plan to use IF it occurs. Passive acceptance: acknowledging the risk and deciding to deal with it IF it occurs (no pre-planned response). Active acceptance is the more mature risk management approach for medium-priority risks.
3
Practice Questions
A quality manager's risk assessment identifies: Risk A — a single-source critical supplier with financial instability (high probability of supply disruption, very high impact). Risk B — a calibration equipment supplier who occasionally ships slightly late (low probability of significant delay, low impact). Which risk response strategies are most appropriate for each?
B is correct. Risk A has high probability × very high impact = highest priority. Strategies: Avoid (qualify and switch to a financially stable alternative supplier) or Mitigate (build safety stock inventory, accelerate alternative supplier qualification, negotiate supply agreements with contractual remedies). Risk B has low probability × low impact = low priority. Accept is the appropriate strategy: the cost of mitigation (e.g., qualifying a backup calibration supplier, carrying extra equipment inventory) would far exceed the impact of occasional minor delays on non-critical calibration equipment.
3
The Risk Matrix — Likelihood × Impact Scoring

The risk matrix is the primary tool for assessing and prioritizing risks. The exam tests how to classify risks and what risk level triggers what response:

📐 Risk Matrix Structure
Impact →
Likelihood ↓		High Impact (5)Med Impact (3)Low Impact (1)
High Likelihood (5)25 — EXTREME15 — HIGH5 — MEDIUM
Med Likelihood (3)15 — HIGH9 — MEDIUM3 — LOW
Low Likelihood (1)5 — MEDIUM3 — LOW1 — LOW
Risk levelScoreRequired response
Extreme15-25Immediate action required; escalate to senior management; dedicated mitigation resources; cannot accept this risk
High9-15Formal risk mitigation plan required; assigned owner; specific timeline; monitoring at management level
Medium4-9Monitor; include in standard management reviews; mitigation desirable but not urgent
Low1-4Accept or monitor; routine management attention
4
Risk Response Strategies
StrategyApproachQuality example
AvoidDon't undertake the activity that creates the riskDecide not to use a single-source supplier for a critical component — avoid the concentration risk entirely by qualifying multiple sources
Reduce / MitigateTake action to lower likelihood, impact, or bothImplement incoming inspection for a high-risk supplier to reduce the impact of their quality failures reaching production
TransferShift the financial impact of the risk to another partyRequire suppliers to carry quality liability insurance; warranty back-to-back clauses in supplier contracts
AcceptAcknowledge the risk and decide to live with it — usually for low-level risks where mitigation cost exceeds risk costAccept the risk of minor cosmetic variation in a non-visible component where the cost of controlling it exceeds any customer impact
5
Additional Practice Questions
A quality manager identifies a risk: "Single-source supplier for a critical safety component — if the supplier cannot deliver, production halts and safety-critical products cannot be shipped." She rates: Likelihood = 2 (supplier has been reliable for 3 years), Impact = 5 (production halt + safety implications). Risk score = 10. How should this risk be classified and managed?
B is correct. Risk score = Likelihood × Impact = 2 × 5 = 10, which falls in the HIGH risk zone (9-15). The critical quality principle: high-impact risks require formal mitigation plans EVEN WHEN likelihood is low. A safety-critical single-source supply failure — even with only 2-in-5 likelihood — has consequences severe enough to demand active risk mitigation: qualifying alternative sources, safety stock, contingency planning. Risk management is NOT about only managing likely events — it is about managing ANY combination of likelihood × impact that produces unacceptable potential consequences. For safety-critical items, even rare risks require formal management.

Section IV Overview

Quality tools are the technical core of the CMQ/OE exam. This section covers the 7 classic tools, 7 management tools, DMAIC, SPC, process capability calculations, measurement systems analysis, acceptance sampling, DOE, and QFD. Calculation questions come primarily from this section.

📋 Exam weight: 29 questions (~18%)
📚 BoK chapters: IV.A, IV.B, IV.C
🧮 Calculation questions: Cp, Cpk, Gauge R&R%, DPMO, ROI

§IV · Topic 1
The 7 Classic Quality Tools

The seven classic (basic) quality tools are the foundation of quality problem-solving. The exam tests: which tool to use for a given purpose, what each tool produces, and key distinctions between similar tools. Most questions present a scenario and ask which tool is most appropriate.

📚 BoK: IV.A
⚠️ Trap risk: High — tool selection and purpose questions
1
The 7 Tools — Complete Reference
ToolWhat it doesWhen to use itKey output
1. FlowchartMaps the sequence of steps in a process — shows how work flows from input to outputUnderstanding or documenting the current process; identifying redundant, missing, or incorrect steps; ISO 9001 process documentationVisual process map showing steps, decision points, and flow
2. Check SheetStructured form for systematically collecting and recording data — tallies frequency of eventsFirst tool in problem-solving: gathering data on how often defects occur, where they occur, when they occurFrequency tally data ready for analysis (often feeds Pareto chart)
3. HistogramBar chart showing the distribution of a continuous variable — frequency of values in defined rangesUnderstanding process variation, distribution shape (normal? skewed? bimodal?), spread, and central tendencyVisual distribution shape — reveals whether data is normally distributed, skewed, or multi-modal
4. Pareto ChartBar chart with categories sorted by frequency (descending) plus cumulative line — shows the vital few vs. useful manyPrioritizing which problems to address first; applying Juran's vital few principle to direct improvement resourcesRanked defect categories with cumulative percentage — typically top 2-3 categories = 70-80% of total
5. Cause-and-Effect Diagram (Fishbone/Ishikawa)Structured brainstorming tool that organizes potential causes into categories (6Ms: Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother Nature/Environment)Generating and organizing hypotheses about what is causing a problem — before data collection to verifyVisual map of potential causes by category — hypotheses for investigation
6. Scatter DiagramPlot of paired data showing relationship between two variables (x vs. y)Investigating whether a relationship exists between a potential cause and a quality outcomeVisual pattern showing correlation direction and strength — or absence of correlation
7. Control ChartTime-series plot with statistical control limits showing process variation over timeMonitoring ongoing process stability — detecting whether variation is common cause (system) or special cause (assignable)Visual of process stability with UCL, LCL, and centerline — signals when to investigate vs. when to leave the process alone
2
Critical Distinctions the Exam Tests
⚠️ Histogram vs. Control Chart — most confused pair
Histogram: Shows distribution of ALL data as a snapshot — shape, spread, central tendency. Does NOT show time sequence. Used to understand process variation characteristics.

Control Chart: Shows individual measurements in TIME SEQUENCE with statistical limits. Used to detect changes in process behavior over time. Cannot show distribution shape directly.

Rule: "What does the distribution look like?" → Histogram. "Is the process stable over time?" → Control Chart.
⚠️ Scatter Diagram — correlation ≠ causation
A scatter diagram shows correlation (relationship between variables) — it does NOT prove causation. Even a strong positive correlation only means the variables move together. A designed experiment (DOE) is needed to establish causation by controlling for other variables.
⚠️ Cause-and-Effect — generates hypotheses, not verified causes
The fishbone diagram is a brainstorming and hypothesis-generation tool. It lists POTENTIAL causes — which must then be verified with data. The fishbone itself cannot tell you which cause is actually responsible. The exam frequently tests this distinction.
⚠️ Pareto — Juran's "vital few" principle
The Pareto chart applies Juran's vital few/useful many principle: typically ~80% of defects come from ~20% of causes. The chart makes this visible by sorting categories in descending frequency. The purpose is NOT to show all causes — it is to identify the FEW causes that account for MOST of the problem, so resources are focused on maximum impact.
3
Tool Selection — Exam Scenarios
ScenarioCorrect toolWhy
"We want to understand how many defects occur and which type is most frequent"Check sheet → then Pareto chartCheck sheet collects the data; Pareto analyzes it for vital few
"We want to see if higher temperature causes more defects"Scatter diagramInvestigating potential cause-effect relationship between two variables
"We want to know if our process output is normally distributed"HistogramDistribution shape is displayed by histogram
"We want to know all the possible reasons this defect might be occurring"Cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagramStructured brainstorming of potential causes
"We want to see if our process has shifted in the last 3 months"Control chartTime-series monitoring detects process shifts
"We want to understand each step in our current inspection process"FlowchartProcess mapping shows steps and sequence
"We want to see which 3 defect types account for most of our customer complaints"Pareto chartVital few identification through ranked frequency display
4
Practice Questions
A quality team is investigating high defect rates on a production line. They want to systematically gather data over two weeks to understand which defect types occur most frequently, on which shifts, and at which workstations. Which tool should they use first to collect this data?
C is correct. The check sheet is the data collection tool — used first to systematically gather the frequency data by category. Once the check sheet data is collected, it feeds the Pareto chart for prioritization analysis. The Pareto chart (A) is the analysis tool, not the data collection tool — you cannot create a Pareto without first collecting the frequency data that a check sheet provides. Fishbone (B) is for generating hypotheses about causes — used AFTER the Pareto identifies WHICH defects to investigate. Histogram (D) displays distribution of continuous data, not categorical frequency counts.
A quality engineer plots oven temperature (X-axis) versus product tensile strength (Y-axis) for 45 production runs. She observes a clear positive linear pattern. Her manager concludes: "Higher oven temperature CAUSES higher tensile strength — we should always run at maximum temperature." What is wrong with this conclusion?
D is correct. Scatter diagrams show correlation — the tendency of two variables to move together. They cannot establish causation. The positive pattern means "when temperature is higher, tensile strength tends to be higher" — not "temperature causes higher strength." A third variable (e.g., a specific material batch that happens to run at higher temperatures AND produces higher tensile strength for independent reasons) could explain the correlation. A designed experiment (DOE) — where temperature is deliberately manipulated while other variables are controlled — is needed to establish causation.
3
Tool Selection Guide — Scenario-Based
Quality problem situationBest toolWhy
Need to identify which defect type causes the most failures (80/20 analysis)Pareto chartRanks categories by frequency; identifies vital few causes
Need to brainstorm all possible causes of a quality problem before investigatingFishbone/IshikawaStructures potential causes by 6M categories; generates hypotheses
Need to verify whether two variables are related (e.g., temperature and defect rate)Scatter diagramShows the relationship (correlation) between two continuous variables
Need to track how often each type of defect occurs on the production floorCheck sheetStructured data collection form; tallies frequencies in real time
Need to understand the distribution and spread of a dimension measurementHistogramShows frequency distribution; reveals shape (normal, skewed, bimodal)
Need to monitor a process over time for out-of-control conditionsControl chartSeparates common-cause from special-cause variation; signals when to investigate
Need to map all steps in a process to identify where errors could occurFlowchart/process mapVisual representation of process steps, decisions, and flow
⚠️ The most commonly confused tool pairs
Fishbone vs. Check sheet: Fishbone = brainstorm POTENTIAL causes (before data is collected). Check sheet = collect DATA on actual occurrences (after deciding what to count).

Histogram vs. Control chart: Histogram = static snapshot of distribution (no time dimension). Control chart = time-ordered display of process performance (shows trends, shifts, patterns over time).

Pareto vs. Histogram: Pareto = categorical data ranked by frequency (defect types). Histogram = continuous data showing distribution (measurement values).

Scatter diagram vs. Control chart: Scatter = relationship between TWO variables. Control = one variable over time vs. control limits.
4
Additional Practice Questions
A quality team has collected 3 months of defect data from a circuit board assembly line. They have categorized all defects into 8 types. They want to focus their improvement effort on the smallest number of defect types that will produce the greatest quality improvement. Which tool should they use, and what principle does it apply?
B is correct. The Pareto chart is specifically designed for this situation: categorical defect data where the goal is to identify the vital few categories driving the majority of the problem. The Pareto Principle (also called the 80/20 rule) states that approximately 80% of problems come from 20% of causes. By ranking the 8 defect types by frequency and displaying them as a bar chart with a cumulative percentage line, the team can immediately see which 1-3 defect types account for 80% of all defects. This focuses improvement resources on the highest-ROI categories rather than spreading effort equally across all 8 types.
A process engineer suspects that curing temperature might be related to the tensile strength of molded parts. She has 30 paired data points (temperature, tensile strength) collected over two weeks. Which tool reveals whether this relationship exists, and what would a specific pattern in the tool's output tell her?
A is correct. The scatter diagram is specifically designed to show the relationship between two continuous variables (temperature and tensile strength). Each data point is plotted as (x=temperature, y=tensile strength). Pattern interpretation: Points trending upward left-to-right = positive correlation (higher temperature → higher strength). Points trending downward = negative correlation. Random scatter = no correlation. Tight cluster around a line = strong correlation. Curved pattern = nonlinear relationship. IMPORTANT: Correlation does not prove causation — a strong positive scatter diagram pattern suggests a relationship worth investigating, not that temperature CAUSES strength changes. DOE (controlled experiment) is needed to confirm causality.
An operator notices that Product X has been running with more defects than usual over the past 2 weeks. She wants to collect systematic data on which specific defect types are occurring and how many of each during each shift, in real time at the workstation. Which tool is most appropriate for immediate use at the workstation?
D is correct. The check sheet is designed for exactly this use case: real-time, at-the-source data collection by operators. It requires no statistical analysis skill to use — the operator simply makes a tally mark in the appropriate category each time a defect type occurs. At the end of the shift, the check sheet provides a count by defect type that can be used to build a Pareto chart (analysis) later. The relationship: Check sheet provides the raw data → Pareto chart analyzes it for prioritization → Fishbone brainstorms causes for the highest-priority category. These tools work sequentially in the quality problem-solving process.
📚 Open-Book Reference: Tague, The Quality Toolbox
The Quality Toolbox contains 63 quality tools organized alphabetically, each with a one-page purpose, procedure, worked example, and variation notes. It is the fastest §IV open-book reference — you can look up any tool by name and find a complete worked example within 30 seconds. Highly recommended as one of your bound references for the December exam.
✦
From Tague — Run Chart vs. Control Chart

Source: Tague, N.R., The Quality Toolbox, 2nd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2004

Tague distinguishes two related but different tools that candidates frequently confuse:

Run ChartControl Chart
What it showsData plotted over time in sequence — reveals trends, shifts, and patternsData plotted over time WITH statistically calculated control limits (UCL, LCL, centerline)
Statistical basisNo control limits — uses run rules (runs above/below median) to detect non-random patternsControl limits at ±3σ from the mean — based on the natural variation of the process
What it detectsNon-random patterns: trends, cycles, clustering, mixtures — before enough data exists for control limitsBoth out-of-control points (beyond limits) AND non-random patterns (Western Electric rules)
When to useEarly in data collection before 20–25 data points are available; when you want a simple time-series display; when control limit calculation is not yet appropriateWhen you have 20–25+ data points and want to formally distinguish common-cause from special-cause variation
Run rules for run charts8+ consecutive points on same side of median = non-random; 6+ consecutive points trending up or down = trendWestern Electric rules (see SPC page) applied to control chart zones
⚠️ The run chart exam trap
The exam may present a "run chart" and test whether you can identify non-random patterns using run chart rules (based on the MEDIAN, not the mean). The control chart runs rules use the MEAN (centerline) and zone structure. Run chart rules use only the median and count of consecutive points above/below it. These are different tests applied to different charts — don't apply control chart zone rules to a run chart.
A quality team has just begun collecting data on a new process. They have 12 data points so far. They want to display the data over time and look for non-random patterns. Which tool is most appropriate at this stage?
C is correct. Tague's guideline: control charts require a minimum of 20–25 data points to establish statistically valid control limits. With only 12 points, the control limits calculated would be unreliable and could either miss real special causes or signal false alarms. A run chart is the appropriate starting tool — it displays the time-ordered data (allowing trend and pattern detection using run rules) without requiring statistically validated limits. Once 20–25 points are collected, the team can convert to a formal control chart with calculated limits.
✦
From Tague — Relations Diagram & Affinity Diagram

Tague documents two management tools that address complex, multi-factor quality problems that the basic 7 tools cannot handle:

ToolPurposeWhen to useQuality application
Affinity DiagramOrganizes large amounts of qualitative data (ideas, opinions, issues) into natural groupings based on their relationshipsAfter brainstorming large numbers of ideas; when the team is overwhelmed by the volume and complexity of issues; VOC data synthesisOrganizing raw VOC data into customer need categories; grouping potential root causes from a brainstorm session before creating a fishbone
Relations Diagram (Interrelationship Digraph)Shows cause-and-effect relationships among many factors — which factors cause other factorsComplex quality problems with many interrelated causes; when you need to identify the "driver" factors that influence many others vs. "outcome" factors that are influenced by manyIdentifying the root-root cause in a multi-layer cause structure; factors with many outgoing arrows are the primary drivers to address
💡 Reading a Relations Diagram — driver vs. outcome identification
In a relations diagram, draw arrows from causes to effects. Count each factor's arrows:

Many outgoing arrows (causes many others): This is a DRIVER — a fundamental root cause that, if addressed, will affect many downstream factors
Many incoming arrows (caused by many others): This is an OUTCOME — a symptom produced by multiple upstream causes

The quality improvement priority: address the DRIVERS first. Addressing outcomes without addressing drivers produces temporary fixes that recur.
✦
Fishbone (Ishikawa) Diagram — Visual Structure

The fishbone is the most visually diagrammed tool in §IV. Know the 6M categories and how causes branch from each bone. Exam questions show a fishbone and ask you to identify the tool, the category of a given cause, or the difference between a fishbone and a 5-Why analysis.

⚠️ Fishbone vs. 5-Why — exam distinction
A fishbone diagram identifies CATEGORIES of potential causes through team brainstorming — it is a breadth tool. The 5-Why analysis drills down on ONE cause to find the ROOT cause — it is a depth tool. They are often used sequentially: (1) use the fishbone to identify the most likely cause category, (2) use 5-Why on the highest-priority cause from the fishbone to reach the root cause. Exam trap: "A fishbone tells you the root cause" — FALSE. It identifies potential causes that must then be verified with data.
✦
Pareto Chart — The 80/20 Rule Visualised

The Pareto chart combines a bar chart with a cumulative percentage line. Know how to read the cumulative line to identify the "vital few" causes that account for ~80% of the problem.

💡 Reading the Pareto chart for exam questions
The cumulative % line crosses 80% between the 2nd and 3rd bars. This means: 2 defect types (Scratches + Dents) account for 70% of all defects — close to the Pareto principle. The quality improvement recommendation: resolve Scratches and Dents first; these "vital few" causes will produce the greatest improvement in overall defect rate. The "useful many" (Misalignment, Colour, Other) can be addressed later. The exam tests whether you can read the cumulative line and identify how many categories fall within the 80% threshold.
§IV · Topic 2
7 Management & Planning Tools

The 7 management and planning tools are used primarily for planning, organizing ideas, and managing complex decisions — not for statistical analysis. The exam tests correct tool selection given a planning or decision scenario.

📚 BoK: IV.A
⚠️ Key trap: Affinity diagram vs. Interrelationship Digraph — both deal with complex ideas but for different purposes
1
The 7 Tools — Complete Reference
ToolPurposeWhen to use
1. Affinity Diagram (KJ Method)Organizes large amounts of qualitative data (ideas, facts, opinions) into natural groupings based on affinity (relationship)After brainstorming when there are many unorganized ideas; VOC analysis; organizing complex data into themes before analysis
2. Interrelationship Digraph (ID)Maps cause-and-effect relationships between many interrelated factors using arrows; identifies drivers (many outgoing arrows) vs. outcomes (many incoming arrows)Complex problems where many factors influence each other; finding root cause drivers in multivariable situations
3. Tree DiagramSystematically breaks down a goal or topic into increasing levels of detail — hierarchical decompositionBreaking a strategic goal into tactics into tasks; fault tree analysis; developing comprehensive action plans
4. Matrix DiagramShows relationships between two or more sets of information in a grid format; cells indicate relationship type/strengthShowing relationships between requirements and solutions; capability vs. requirement mapping; cross-functional responsibility assignment
5. Prioritization MatrixUses weighted criteria to objectively rank options against each other; combines multiple criteria into a single priority scoreSelecting from multiple improvement options when criteria have different weights; making complex multi-criteria decisions
6. Process Decision Program Chart (PDPC)Anticipates what can go wrong in implementing a plan and pre-identifies countermeasures — "what if" planningRisk planning for complex implementations; new process introduction; contingency planning
7. Activity Network Diagram (AND / Arrow Diagram)Shows the sequence and timing of tasks with dependencies — identifies critical pathComplex project scheduling; determining minimum project duration; identifying which tasks cannot be delayed
2
Key Distinctions
⚠️ Affinity Diagram vs. Interrelationship Digraph
Affinity Diagram: Groups ideas into themes — used when you have many unorganized ideas and need to see what naturally belongs together. No arrows or causality — just grouping.

Interrelationship Digraph: Maps cause-and-effect arrows between factors — used when you have identified multiple factors and need to understand which are drivers (root causes) and which are outcomes (effects). Uses directional arrows.

Exam signal: "organize ideas into themes" → Affinity. "Find which factor is the root driver among many interrelated factors" → Interrelationship Digraph.
⚠️ PDPC vs. Risk Register
PDPC (Process Decision Program Chart) is a visual tool that maps the implementation plan and for each step asks "what could go wrong?" with pre-planned countermeasures. It is a proactive planning tool. A Risk Register is a document that lists, scores, and tracks risks. The exam will test PDPC as the tool for anticipating implementation problems and pre-planning responses.
3
Practice Questions
A quality improvement team has just completed a brainstorming session and generated 67 ideas for improving the customer complaint handling process. The ideas are on sticky notes scattered on a wall with no organization. Which tool should the team use next?
B is correct. The affinity diagram (KJ method) is specifically designed for organizing large volumes of unstructured qualitative data into natural groupings. 67 unorganized brainstorming ideas on sticky notes is the classic affinity diagram use case. The process: team members silently sort ideas into groups based on perceived affinity → groups are given header titles → themes emerge from the organized groupings. This creates order from brainstorming chaos before analysis tools (like the interrelationship digraph or prioritization matrix) can be effectively applied.
A quality team has identified 8 factors contributing to a high defect rate: operator fatigue, material inconsistency, machine vibration, measurement error, temperature variation, procedure ambiguity, shift handoff problems, and inspection gaps. They need to determine which factors are root cause DRIVERS versus which are downstream EFFECTS. Which tool is most appropriate?
D is correct. The Interrelationship Digraph maps directional cause-and-effect relationships among multiple interrelated factors. For each pair of factors, the team draws an arrow from the cause to the effect. After all relationships are mapped, counting arrows: factors with more outgoing arrows than incoming arrows are ROOT CAUSE DRIVERS — they influence many other factors. Factors with more incoming arrows are OUTCOMES — they are being driven by other factors. This reveals the true root causes in complex multivariable situations where simple fishbone analysis misses the interactions.
✦
From Tague — Tree Diagram & Matrix Diagram in Depth

Source: Tague, N.R., The Quality Toolbox, 2nd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2004

ToolStructureQuality use caseKey output
Tree DiagramHierarchical branching from general goals to increasingly specific tasks/means. Each branch answers "How do we achieve the level above?"Deploying a quality objective into specific actions; breaking down a complex quality problem into manageable sub-problems; Hoshin Kanri deployment of quality goals to action itemsComplete set of specific, actionable tasks needed to achieve a high-level quality goal — no gaps, no overlaps
Matrix DiagramGrid showing relationships between two or more sets of items using relationship symbols (strong ●, medium ○, weak △, none = blank)QFD House of Quality (customer needs × engineering characteristics); responsibility matrix (RACI); supplier evaluation (suppliers × criteria); root cause analysis (causes × effects)Visual relationship map that shows which factors are most strongly related — guides prioritization of where to focus improvement effort
Prioritization MatrixWeighted decision matrix comparing options against weighted criteria — quantifies which option best satisfies multiple objectives simultaneouslySupplier selection among multiple qualified candidates; selecting among competing quality improvement project proposals; choosing between alternative corrective action approachesObjective ranking of options that makes complex multi-criteria decisions transparent and defensible
💡 Matrix diagram relationship symbols — exam tested
◉ or ● = Strong relationship (weight: 9)
○ = Moderate relationship (weight: 3)
△ = Weak relationship (weight: 1)
Blank = No relationship (weight: 0)

These weights are used in QFD House of Quality to calculate which engineering characteristics most strongly impact customer requirements. The column with the highest weighted total is the engineering characteristic most critical to customer quality perception — and therefore the highest-priority design focus.
§IV · Topic 3
DMAIC Methodology

DMAIC (Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control) is the Six Sigma improvement methodology. The exam tests: what happens in each phase, which tools are used in each phase, and what is the critical difference between phases — especially Measure vs. Analyze, and Improve vs. Control.

📚 BoK: IV.B
⚠️ Key trap: Control phase is NOT optional — without it, improvements revert
1
The Five Phases — What Happens and When
PhaseCore questionKey activitiesKey tools
DefineWhat is the problem and what does success look like?Define the problem precisely; establish project scope; identify customers and their requirements; build the project charter; create SIPOCProject charter; SIPOC; VOC; Kano model; stakeholder analysis
MeasureHow bad is it right now, and can we trust our measurement?Validate the measurement system (Gauge R&R); establish baseline process performance (Cp, Cpk, sigma level, DPMO); identify key input and output variablesGauge R&R; Cp/Cpk calculation; control charts; process mapping; DPMO calculation
AnalyzeWhat is causing the problem?Analyze data to identify root causes; test hypotheses with statistical tools; confirm the vital few root causes that explain most of the variationFishbone diagram; Pareto chart; hypothesis testing; regression analysis; FMEA; scatter diagrams
ImproveHow do we fix the root causes?Generate and evaluate solution alternatives; pilot the best solution; validate improvement with data; implement validated solutionDOE; poka-yoke; solution matrix; piloting; FMEA for solutions
ControlHow do we sustain the improvement permanently?Update SOPs and work instructions; implement control charts for ongoing monitoring; train operators; define response plan for out-of-control signals; transfer ownership to process owner; close projectControl charts; updated SOPs; control plan; response plan; training materials
2
Critical Phase Distinctions
⚠️ Measure vs. Analyze — the most confused phases
Measure: Quantifies the CURRENT STATE — how bad is the problem right now? Validates measurement system. Establishes the baseline. No cause analysis here.

Analyze: Identifies ROOT CAUSES — what is CAUSING the baseline to be what it is? Uses the data collected in Measure to find the why.

Rule: "Establish how bad" → Measure. "Find out why it's bad" → Analyze.
⚠️ The Control phase is not optional
The single most common DMAIC failure in quality organizations: closing the project after Improve. Without Control phase work (updated SOPs, control charts, response plans, operator training), improvements revert within 6-18 months when the project team disbands, personnel changes, or production pressure mounts. This is the Kotter Step 8 failure applied to DMAIC — not anchoring the change.
💡 SIPOC — used in Define, not Analyze
The SIPOC (Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers) is a high-level process map created in the Define phase to establish scope and boundaries. It is NOT a detailed process analysis tool — that comes later. The exam tests that SIPOC = Define phase tool.
3
Practice Questions
A DMAIC team has completed the Analyze phase and identified three verified root causes. The project sponsor wants to immediately begin implementing solutions. A quality manager objects, saying the team needs to complete one more activity before implementing. What activity is she referring to?
A is correct. Knowing the root causes (completed in Analyze) does not mean you automatically know the best solution. The Improve phase requires: generating multiple solution alternatives for each root cause, evaluating alternatives using criteria (effectiveness, cost, feasibility, sustainability), selecting the best option, piloting/testing the solution, and validating that it achieves the improvement objective with data. Jumping from identified root causes directly to implementation skips the structured solution design and validation process that Improve provides.
A quality improvement project reduces a critical process defect rate from 8.2% to 1.1% — a 87% improvement verified during the Improve phase. The project is closed and the team disbands. Fourteen months later, the defect rate has returned to 7.8%. Which DMAIC phase failure does this represent?
A is correct. A validated 87% improvement that reverts 14 months later is the classic Control phase failure. The improvement was real — confirmed during Improve phase. But without Control phase elements (updated documented procedures that new operators follow, control charts that detect early reversion, a response plan that triggers action when the process starts to drift, and formal transfer of process ownership), the improvement has no institutional infrastructure to sustain it. Personnel changes, production pressure, and time erode the improvement without these anchoring mechanisms.
3
DMAIC Tools by Phase
PhaseKey outputsPrimary tools
DefineProject charter; problem statement; SIPOC; VOC; CTQ tree; stakeholder analysisProject charter template; SIPOC diagram; affinity diagram (VOC); CTQ flowdown; RACI matrix
MeasureProcess map; baseline capability data; measurement system validation; Y=f(X) identificationProcess flowchart; Gauge R&R; control charts (baseline); data collection plan; Cp/Cpk (baseline); FMEA (initial)
AnalyzeRoot causes verified with data; process variation sources identified; vital few Xs confirmedFishbone/Ishikawa; Pareto chart; 5 Whys; hypothesis testing; regression analysis; scatter diagram; Kepner-Tregoe; value-added analysis
ImproveSolutions designed, piloted, and implemented; new Cpk demonstrated; pilot dataDOE; solution matrix; mistake-proofing (poka-yoke); kaizen events; FMEA (updated); implementation plan
ControlControl plan; updated work instructions; monitoring system; knowledge transfer to process ownerControl chart (ongoing); control plan; standard work; mistake-proofing; visual management; response plan; dashboard
⚠️ DMAIC vs. DMADV — when to use each
DMAIC (Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control): Used to IMPROVE an EXISTING process that is not meeting requirements. The process exists; it is underperforming.

DMADV / DFSS (Design for Six Sigma): Used to CREATE a NEW process or product from scratch, or when a DMAIC improvement reveals the process is so fundamentally broken that incremental improvement cannot fix it — redesign from scratch is needed.

Exam signal: "The process has been improved 3 times with DMAIC but cannot reach Cpk 1.33" → switch to DFSS. "The organization is launching an entirely new service" → DFSS/DMADV.
4
Additional Practice Questions
A Black Belt is leading a DMAIC project to reduce invoice processing errors. In the Analyze phase, her team conducts a fishbone session and identifies 12 potential root causes. She needs to narrow these to the "vital few" actual root causes before moving to Improve. Which tool should she use next to determine which potential causes are actually driving the defects with data?
D is correct. The fishbone diagram generates HYPOTHETICAL causes — it is a brainstorming tool, not an analysis tool. Moving from Analyze brainstorming to data validation is the critical next step: collect data that allows you to test whether each potential cause actually correlates with the defect rate. Stratify data by the suspected cause variables (e.g., does invoice error rate differ by operator? By customer type? By system?). Use scatter diagrams for continuous X variables. This analysis separates the verified vital few root causes from the trivial many — so that Improve phase solutions address the real causes, not hypothetical ones. Moving directly to DOE (B) without verifying root causes wastes resources designing experiments on unconfirmed X variables.
✦
DMAIC Cycle — Tools at Each Phase

The DMAIC roadmap is the most tested §IV methodology. The exam frequently asks which tool belongs in which phase and what each phase PRODUCES (not just does). Know the key output/deliverable of each phase.

⚠️ DMAIC tool placement — most tested exam pattern
The exam presents a scenario and asks "which DMAIC phase is this tool used in?" Know these specific placements:

SIPOC → Define only (not Measure or Analyse)
Gauge R&R → Measure only (before collecting process data, not after)
Fishbone → Analyse (generates hypotheses) — then 5-Why drills into them
DOE → Improve (tests solutions) — not Analyse
Control chart → Measure (baseline) AND Control (ongoing monitoring) — it spans two phases
FMEA → Improve (updated after root cause identified) AND Control (sustained in control plan)
§IV · Topic 4
Statistical Process Control (SPC)

SPC is the most tested statistical topic in §IV. The exam tests: the fundamental distinction between common and special cause variation, control chart rules, chart selection, and what action to take when a signal appears.

📚 BoK: IV.C
⚠️ Key trap: "Within control limits" does NOT mean "in statistical control" — non-random patterns signal special causes even within limits
1
Common Cause vs. Special Cause Variation

Shewhart's fundamental insight — which Deming built his philosophy upon:

Common Cause VariationSpecial Cause Variation
Also calledRandom variation, chance causes, system variationAssignable causes, non-random variation
SourceInherent in the process system — the combined effect of many small, always-present factorsSpecific identifiable factor(s) that are not part of the normal process — a shift, an event, a change
Pattern on control chartPoints scattered randomly within control limits — no patternsPoints outside control limits OR non-random patterns within limits
Responsible partyManagement — only management can change the process systemOperators/local team — can often identify and address the specific cause
Correct responseDo NOT adjust the process — adjust only if you redesign the system. Reacting to common cause as if it were special = tampering.Investigate and eliminate the specific assignable cause
Deming's estimate85-94% of quality problems are common cause (system)6-15% are special cause (assignable)
⚠️ Tampering — the danger of treating common cause as special
When operators react to every common-cause variation by adjusting the process (tightening a setting, changing a parameter), they are tampering. Tampering actually INCREASES variation because you are adding variation to a system that was already in its natural state. This is why the control chart exists: to signal WHEN to react (special cause) and WHEN to leave the process alone (common cause).
2
Control Chart Structure
ElementMeaningCalculated as
Centerline (CL)Process average — where the process is centeredMean of all subgroup averages (X̄)
Upper Control Limit (UCL)Upper boundary for random variation — 3 standard deviations above centerCL + 3σ
Lower Control Limit (LCL)Lower boundary for random variation — 3 standard deviations below centerCL − 3σ
💡 Why 3 sigma limits?
At 3σ limits, the probability of a point falling outside the limits by random chance alone is approximately 0.27% (3 in 1,000). This is low enough that when a point falls outside, it is very likely a special cause — not random variation. The 3σ rule balances Type I errors (false signals) with Type II errors (missed signals).
3
Western Electric Rules — Non-Random Patterns

The control chart signals special causes in two ways: (1) points outside control limits, AND (2) non-random patterns within control limits. The most commonly tested patterns:

Pattern (Western Electric Rule)SignalProbability if random
1 point outside control limits (above UCL or below LCL)Special cause — investigate immediately0.27%
8 or more consecutive points on ONE SIDE of the centerline (a "run")Process mean has shifted — investigate cause of shift(0.5)⁸ = 0.39%
6 consecutive points steadily increasing or decreasing (a "trend")Process is drifting — investigate cause of trend (tool wear, material depletion)Very low probability by chance
2 out of 3 consecutive points in Zone A (beyond 2σ from centerline, same side)Process may be shifting — warning signalLow probability by chance
⚠️ The most important run rule exam trap
A scenario will show: "The last 9 points are all above the centerline but none exceed the UCL." A colleague says "it's in control — all points are within limits." This is WRONG. Eight or more consecutive points on one side of the centerline is a non-random pattern signaling a process shift — an out-of-control condition even though no point has exceeded a control limit.
4
Control Chart Selection
Data typeChartWhen to use
Variable (continuous measurement)X̄-R chart (X-bar and Range)Subgroups of 2-10 measurements; most common for manufacturing measurements
Variable (continuous)X̄-S chart (X-bar and Standard Deviation)Larger subgroups (n > 10); uses standard deviation instead of range
Variable (individual measurements)I-MR chart (Individuals and Moving Range)One measurement per time period; batch processes; destructive testing
Attribute (proportion defective)p-chartFraction nonconforming; variable sample size acceptable
Attribute (count defective)np-chartNumber of nonconforming items; requires constant sample size
Attribute (count of defects per unit)c-chartCount of defects in a constant inspection area/opportunity
Attribute (count of defects per unit, variable area)u-chartAverage defects per unit; variable inspection area
5
Practice Questions
A quality engineer plots an X̄-R control chart for a shaft diameter process. The last 10 subgroup averages are: 25.01, 25.02, 25.03, 25.02, 25.04, 25.03, 25.04, 25.05, 25.04, 25.05. All points are within control limits (UCL=25.08, LCL=24.92). A production supervisor says "the process is in statistical control." The quality engineer disagrees. Who is correct?
A is correct. Two non-random patterns are present: (1) A run of 10 consecutive points on one side of the centerline — the Western Electric rule signals out-of-control at 8+ consecutive points on one side. (2) A trend of 6 consecutive increasing points (25.01 → 25.02 → 25.03 → 25.02 → 25.04 → 25.03 → 25.04 → 25.05 → 25.04 → 25.05 — the overall trend is upward). Both patterns have very low probability of occurring by chance alone. Statistical control requires BOTH absence of points outside limits AND absence of non-random patterns — the supervisor's definition is incomplete and incorrect.
An operator notices that her process measurement occasionally reads slightly high. Every time she sees a reading above the process average, she adjusts the process down. Every time she sees a reading below average, she adjusts up. Inspection data shows that variation has INCREASED since she began this practice. Which concept explains this outcome?
C is correct. This is the classic tampering scenario. The operator is reacting to common cause variation (normal random scatter around the process mean) as if it were a special cause signal requiring action. Each adjustment introduces additional variation: she moves the process slightly high to compensate for a low reading, then slightly low to compensate for the resulting high reading. Deming famously demonstrated this with the funnel experiment — tampering always increases variation in a stable process. The correct action: establish a control chart and react only to actual statistical signals (points outside limits or non-random patterns), not to individual deviations from the average.
6
Control Chart Interpretation — Complete Run Rule Reference

The Western Electric rules define specific non-random patterns that signal special causes even when no point exceeds the control limits. Control limits divide the chart into zones (Zone A: 2-3σ from center, Zone B: 1-2σ, Zone C: 0-1σ):

RulePatternWhat it signals
Rule 11 point beyond 3σ (outside control limits)Immediate special cause — investigate immediately
Rule 22 of 3 consecutive points in Zone A (beyond 2σ), same sideProcess may be shifting — early warning
Rule 34 of 5 consecutive points in Zone B or beyond (beyond 1σ), same sideProcess is shifting toward one side — investigate
Rule 48 consecutive points on the same side of the centerline (a RUN)Process mean has shifted — most commonly tested run rule
Rule 56 consecutive points steadily increasing or decreasing (a TREND)Process is drifting — investigate (tool wear, material depletion, operator fatigue)
Rule 615 consecutive points in Zone C (within 1σ of centerline) on either sideStratification — data is artificially centered; may indicate mixed populations, sampling error, or tampering
⚠️ The stratification pattern — often overlooked
Rule 6 (15 points all within 1σ of center) looks "too good" — but it actually signals a problem. Natural random variation produces a spread of points across the zones. When all points cluster near the center, it typically means two mixed data sources (two shifts, two machines, two measurement systems) are being plotted together — each individually off-center in opposite directions. The mixing creates an artificially centered pattern. Solution: stratify the data by source and plot each separately.
7
Additional SPC Practice Questions
An X̄-R control chart for a filling process shows the last 30 points: all within control limits, but the last 6 points form a clear downward trend (each one lower than the previous). A production manager says "the process is in control — all points are within limits." A quality engineer objects. Who is correct, and what action is needed?
D is correct. Western Electric Rule 5: 6 consecutive points steadily increasing or decreasing = out-of-control trend signal, regardless of whether points exceed control limits. The trend means the process is systematically drifting in one direction — which will eventually cause points to exceed the LCL if the downward trend continues. Common causes: gradual tool wear reducing fill level, raw material depletion changing viscosity, environmental temperature change affecting the process. The correct response: investigate the trend cause immediately (don't wait for a point to exceed limits) and identify and eliminate the drift cause before process capability is compromised.
A pharmaceutical mixing process produces batches once per day. Only one measurement per batch is possible (destructive testing). The quality engineer wants to implement SPC. Which control chart type should she use?
C is correct. The I-MR (Individuals and Moving Range) chart is specifically designed for situations where: (1) only one measurement is produced per time period, (2) subgroup sampling is impossible (destructive testing means you can only test one unit per batch), or (3) the process produces one product at a time rather than in subgroups. The X̄-R chart requires multiple measurements per subgroup (typically 3-10). With only one measurement per batch, no range can be calculated within a subgroup, so the I-MR uses the moving range (difference between consecutive individual measurements) as the variation estimate.
A quality engineer is monitoring the proportion of defective units coming off a production line. The sample size varies between 200 and 350 units per shift due to production schedule variation. Which control chart should she use?
D is correct. Chart selection rule: when monitoring PROPORTION defective (fraction nonconforming = defective count / sample size) with VARIABLE sample size → p-chart. The p-chart can handle variable sample sizes because each plotted point is the proportion (not the count), and the control limits adjust (widen or narrow) based on each point's sample size — smaller samples have wider limits because they have more sampling uncertainty. The np-chart also monitors proportion defective but requires CONSTANT sample size. Since sample size varies (200-350), only the p-chart is appropriate.
✦
Control Chart — Zones and Out-of-Control Signals

The CMQ/OE exam regularly presents control chart graphs and asks you to identify whether the process is in control, which Western Electric rule is violated, and what type of investigation is needed. Know all four zones and all eight run rules.

Western Electric RuleSignalInterpretation
Rule 11 point beyond ±3σ (UCL or LCL)Special cause — large, sudden shift; investigate immediately
Rule 28 consecutive points same side of CLSustained process shift (mean has moved); investigate process change
Rule 36 consecutive points trending in one directionProcess drift — tool wear, operator fatigue, raw material change
Rule 42 of 3 consecutive points in Zone A (beyond ±2σ) same sideLarge process shift; less dramatic than Rule 1 but still signals special cause
Rule 54 of 5 consecutive points in Zone B or beyond same sideModerate process shift; the average has moved to one side
Rule 615 consecutive points within Zone C (±1σ of CL)Stratification — data is too close to CL; suggests mixed subgroups or data from two processes
Rule 714 consecutive points alternating up and downSystematic pattern — over-adjustment, two alternating machines, or two operators
Rule 88 consecutive points with none in Zone CMixture — data avoids the centre; suggests two different process distributions
§IV · Topic 5
Process Capability (Cp and Cpk)

Process capability questions are the most calculation-heavy on the exam. You WILL get calculations. Understand the formulas, know the interpretation thresholds, and master the critical difference between Cp (potential capability) and Cpk (actual capability accounting for centering).

📚 BoK: IV.C
🧮 Calculation required
⚠️ Key trap: Cp can look good while Cpk reveals the process is off-center and producing defects
1
The Formulas
📐 FORMULAS — Memorize These
Cp (Potential Capability — assumes perfect centering):
Cp = (USL − LSL) / (6σ)

Cpu (Upper capability index):
Cpu = (USL − X̄) / (3σ)

Cpl (Lower capability index):
Cpl = (X̄ − LSL) / (3σ)

Cpk (Actual Capability — takes centering into account):
Cpk = minimum of (Cpu, Cpl)

Key: Cpk always ≤ Cp. When the process is perfectly centered, Cpk = Cp. When off-center, Cpk < Cp.
2
Interpretation Thresholds
Cp or Cpk valueInterpretationAction
< 1.00Incapable — process spread exceeds specification; producing defectsImmediate action required — reduce variation or widen spec (if possible)
