How customers are treated IS a quality dimension — courtesy, active listening, empathy, and responsiveness are quality characteristics of the service delivery process.
2
Practice Questions
A customer complaint analysis reveals that 71% of all complaints relate to how staff treated customers — tone, failure to listen, slow response to questions — rather than to product technical failures. The VP of Operations dismisses the findings: "Those are personality issues, not quality problems. Quality management should focus on defect rates." Which principle from the handbook most directly refutes this position?
A is correct. The handbook's customer-focused organizations section explicitly lists customer service principles as quality management responsibilities. When 71% of complaints relate to service treatment rather than technical failures, the quality management system has a service quality problem — not merely an HR training issue. The quality manager should analyze these complaints, identify root causes (inadequate service quality standards? Lack of accountability? Missing service delivery processes?), and develop corrective actions. Limiting "quality" to technical defect rates misses a large portion of what creates or destroys customer satisfaction.
✦
Service Recovery Paradox — Visual Model

The service recovery paradox is a frequently tested §V concept: a customer who experiences a problem AND receives an excellent recovery can end up MORE satisfied and loyal than a customer who experienced no problem at all.

Recovery elementWhat it requiresWhy it drives the paradox
SpeedRespond to the complaint within a defined, short timeframe — first response within hours, not daysCustomers expect organisations to take complaints seriously; slow response amplifies the original failure
AcknowledgementTake responsibility clearly — do not deflect blame onto the customer or external factorsCustomers feel heard; reduces emotional escalation; the opposite of defensive response
EmpathyRecognise the customer's experience and inconvenience — personalise the responseCustomers who feel understood are significantly more forgiving than those who receive a scripted, impersonal response
Compensation/FixResolve the original problem AND compensate for the inconvenience (refund, replacement, upgrade)The tangible fix demonstrates commitment; the compensation signals that the organisation values the relationship over the transaction
Follow-upCheck that the resolution was satisfactory after the factFollow-up converts a transaction (complaint resolved) into a relationship (we care about your experience)
⚠️ The paradox only works once
Research shows the service recovery paradox only operates on the FIRST failure and recovery with a given customer. A second failure from the same organisation destroys trust permanently — the customer no longer believes the first recovery was genuine. Quality managers must use service recovery data to identify systemic process failures and eliminate their root causes, not just to manage individual complaints. Recovery is a short-term retention tool; prevention is the long-term quality strategy.
§VI · Supply Chain
Section VI Overview

Supply chain management ensures that purchased materials and services meet quality requirements. The exam tests supplier selection criteria, performance measurement, risk management, corrective action, certification, and logistics practices.

📋 Exam weight: 17 questions (~10%)
📚 BoK: VI.A through VI.G
Topics
Supplier Selection & Approval
Supplier Performance Measurement — 4 dimensions
Supplier Risk Management — concentration, financial, quality risk
Supplier Communication & Improvement — SCAR, corrective action
Supplier Certification — requirements, ship-to-stock
Logistics & Material Acceptance — incoming inspection, JIT
§VI · Topic 1
Supplier Selection & Approval
📚 BoK: VI.A
⚠️ Trap: Price alone is NOT a sufficient selection criterion (Deming Point 4)
1
Selection Criteria
CriterionWhat it assesses
Quality capabilityProcess capability (Cpk), quality system maturity, defect history, certification status
Technical competencyUnderstanding of specifications, engineering capability, problem-solving ability
Delivery performanceOn-time delivery history, lead time reliability, capacity
Financial stabilityAbility to sustain the supply relationship; not at risk of sudden closure
Service responsivenessCommunication quality, corrective action responsiveness, technical support
⚠️ Deming Point 4 — End the practice of awarding business on price alone
The handbook (consistent with Deming's 14 Points) explicitly rejects price as the primary selection criterion. Total cost of ownership = purchase price + quality costs (rework, scrap, warranty from poor supplier quality) + logistics costs + risk costs. A cheap supplier with poor quality often costs more in total than a higher-priced reliable supplier.
2
Practice Questions
A purchasing manager selects a new supplier for a critical component based solely on their 15% lower unit price compared to the incumbent. The quality manager objects. Three months later, incoming rejection rates for the new supplier's components reach 12%, requiring extensive inspection, rework, and two production line stoppages. Which quality management principle does this situation illustrate?
D is correct. This illustrates Deming's Point 4 and the total cost of ownership principle from the handbook. The 15% unit price savings was meaningless against: incoming inspection costs, rework labor, scrap materials, production line stoppage costs, expedited orders to compensate for yield loss, and management time on corrective actions. Quality capability should have been evaluated before the selection decision — not discovered through production failure. The handbook's supplier selection criteria explicitly include quality capability, delivery performance, and financial stability precisely because price alone is an incomplete and misleading selection basis.
3
The Supplier Approval Process

Selection is followed by a formal approval process before a supplier can provide materials for production:

StageActivityOutput
1. Identify candidatesMarket research, existing relationships, trade publications, referralsCandidate list for evaluation
2. Initial screeningReview supplier capability questionnaire; check certifications (ISO 9001, IATF 16949); review financial healthShort list of qualified candidates for detailed evaluation
3. Quality system survey/auditDetailed assessment of supplier's quality management system against defined criteria; may include on-site audit (2nd-party audit)Quality system rating/score; identification of gaps
4. Sample qualificationSupplier produces samples; customer verifies dimensional, functional, and reliability requirements; Cpk studies on critical characteristicsApproved samples; process capability data
5. Formal approvalQuality manager approves supplier on approved supplier list (ASL); defines supply conditions, inspection requirements, and performance expectationsSupplier on ASL; inspection plan defined
6. Ongoing monitoringTrack quality, delivery, cost, and service performance; periodic re-qualification for critical suppliersSupplier performance scorecard; continuous supply assurance
4
Weighted Criteria Supplier Selection

When multiple suppliers are being evaluated, a weighted criteria matrix provides an objective, data-driven selection decision:

📋 Weighted Criteria Example

Three suppliers evaluated against 5 criteria (0-10 score each):

CriterionWeightSupplier ASupplier BSupplier C
Quality capability (Cpk, history)35%9 → 3.157 → 2.456 → 2.10
Financial stability20%8 → 1.609 → 1.805 → 1.00
Delivery performance20%7 → 1.408 → 1.609 → 1.80
Price/Total cost15%6 → 0.908 → 1.2010 → 1.50
Service responsiveness10%9 → 0.907 → 0.706 → 0.60
TOTAL SCORE100%7.957.757.00

Supplier C has the lowest price but the lowest total weighted score. Supplier A wins despite higher cost because quality capability (weighted 35%) is a priority. The weighting structure reflects the organization's quality strategy: quality risk carries more weight than unit price.

⚠️ The weighted criteria exam trap
The exam will present a scenario where the lowest-cost supplier scores highest on price but lowest overall due to poor quality and service scores. The question tests whether you recognize that the weighted total (not any single criterion) should drive the selection. Organizations that override the weighted score because "Supplier C is cheapest" are reverting to price-alone selection — which Deming's Point 4 explicitly rejects.
5
Additional Practice Questions
A quality manager has completed supplier evaluations. Supplier X: Quality = 9.5, Delivery = 9.0, Price = 6.5, Financial stability = 4.0. Supplier Y: Quality = 7.5, Delivery = 8.0, Price = 9.5, Financial stability = 9.0. The purchasing manager argues for Supplier Y because "the numbers average out the same and Y is cheaper." The quality manager objects. What is the quality-specific concern about Supplier Y?
D is correct. This scenario illustrates why simple averages are insufficient for supplier selection — they mask critical differences in specific criteria. Supplier X: excellent quality and delivery but financially fragile (risk of sudden supply disruption or quality deterioration from financial distress). Supplier Y: financially solid but lower quality (risk of incoming nonconformances affecting production). For a critical, safety-important material, Supplier X's quality advantage might outweigh its financial risk. For a commodity material where alternatives exist, Supplier Y's financial stability might matter more. The weighted criteria approach forces the organization to make the weighting decision explicitly — based on risk priorities — rather than hiding it in an "average" that obscures the trade-off.
📚 Additional References: Bossert & Durivage
Bossert, Supplier Management Handbook: Full supplier qualification process with detailed criteria matrices, sample evaluation forms, and rating systems. Best open-book reference for §VI qualification and performance questions — tab to the supplier qualification chapter.

Durivage, CSQP Handbook: Modern supplier quality risk assessment, advanced outsourcing quality management, supply chain risk frameworks — most current supply chain quality reference available.
✦
From Bossert — Supplier Evaluation Criteria Framework

Source: Bossert, J.L., Supplier Management Handbook, 6th ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2004

Bossert presents a comprehensive supplier evaluation framework that goes beyond simple quality ratings to assess total supplier capability:

Evaluation domainSpecific criteriaWhy it predicts quality outcomes
Quality SystemQuality management system certification (ISO 9001, IATF 16949, AS9100); internal audit program effectiveness; CAPA system maturity; quality planning capabilityMature QMS predicts consistent product quality; certification indicates minimum system requirements are met
Technical CapabilityProcess capability (Cpk on critical characteristics); equipment calibration and maintenance; measurement system adequacy (Gauge R&R results); design capability (if applicable)Process capability data provides statistical evidence of ability to produce to specification consistently
Financial HealthCredit ratings; revenue trends; profitability; debt-to-equity ratio; customer concentration riskFinancially distressed suppliers cut quality investment; financial failure disrupts supply; concentration risk means one lost customer could destabilize the supplier
Management & OrganizationQuality management leadership quality; turnover rate in quality functions; training investment; quality culture indicatorsQuality culture and leadership stability predict sustained quality performance better than point-in-time audit scores
Delivery PerformanceOn-time delivery history; lead time reliability; capacity vs. demand; production scheduling systemsDelivery performance under stress (at full capacity) predicts whether quality is maintained when schedule pressure increases
Continuous ImprovementDocumented CI program; year-over-year quality performance trends; proactive problem identification; benchmarking activitiesA supplier improving year-over-year is a better long-term partner than one with good current performance but no improvement trajectory
A quality team is evaluating two suppliers for a critical safety component. Supplier A: ISO 9001 certified, Cpk = 1.65 on critical dimensions, revenue declining 15% annually, no documented continuous improvement program. Supplier B: IATF 16949 certified, Cpk = 1.42, financially stable with growing revenue, active Six Sigma program. Using Bossert's supplier evaluation framework, which supplier presents lower total risk and why?
B is correct. Bossert's principle: supplier evaluation must be forward-looking, not just current-state assessment. Supplier A's 15% annual revenue decline is a red flag: declining revenue typically leads to reduced workforce, deferred capital investment, and quality system erosion as cost-cutting measures. A supplier with a high current Cpk but deteriorating financial health is a known pattern for future quality failures — the quality system weakens before the Cpk numbers show it. Supplier B's active CI program indicates the Cpk of 1.42 is a floor being actively improved rather than a ceiling. For a safety-critical component, the combination of financial stability and a CI trajectory makes Supplier B the lower-risk long-term partner, even with slightly lower current capability.
✦
Supply Chain Structure — Tier Diagram

Understanding the multi-tier supply chain structure is essential for answering §VI questions on supplier risk, sub-tier management, and quality flow-down requirements.

Figure 4: Multi-Tier Supply Chain — quality risk increases with distance from Tier 1

Supplier tierRelationshipQuality management approachRisk level
Tier 1Direct suppliers — you purchase directly from them; full contractual relationshipFull qualification, scorecards, QBRs, SCARs, incoming inspection, capability studies, supplier auditsManaged — high visibility
Tier 2Your suppliers' suppliers — indirect relationship; quality requirements must be "flowed down" through Tier 1Quality flow-down clauses in Tier 1 contracts; Tier 1 accountable for Tier 2 management; spot audits of critical Tier 2 suppliersElevated — limited visibility
Tier 3Often invisible — raw material and component producers feeding Tier 2Supply chain mapping to identify critical Tier 3 relationships; dual-source requirements for critical materials at Tier 3High — minimal visibility; major source of supply disruptions
A medical device manufacturer discovers that two of its three Tier 1 contract manufacturers both source a critical bio-compatible polymer from the same single Tier 3 raw material supplier — a fact unknown to the quality team until a supply disruption occurs. Which quality management principle was not applied, and what should have been done proactively?
C is correct. This is the classic sub-tier risk scenario from Durivage's CSQP Handbook. The quality failure was not a product quality failure — it was a supply chain design failure: hidden concentration risk at Tier 3 that invalidated the apparent redundancy of having multiple Tier 1 suppliers. Supply chain mapping is the proactive tool: require Tier 1 suppliers to document their critical sub-tier sources during qualification; then map the full network to identify where multiple supply chains converge at a single Tier 2 or Tier 3 node. When a single-source critical material is identified, the risk response is either dual-sourcing (qualify an alternate Tier 3 supplier through the Tier 1 suppliers) or strategic safety stock. Incoming inspection (D) catches product quality problems but provides no protection against supply disruption — you cannot inspect your way to supply continuity.
§VI · Topic 2
Supplier Performance Measurement
📚 BoK: VI.D
⚠️ Key: 4 dimensions — Quality, Cost, Delivery, Service
1
The Four Performance Dimensions
DimensionKey metrics
QualityIncoming defect rate (ppm or %), lot rejection rate, Cpk of supplied materials, corrective action completion rate
CostPrice competitiveness vs. market, cost reduction year-over-year, total cost of ownership
DeliveryOn-time delivery percentage, lead time reliability, responsiveness to schedule changes
ServiceTechnical support quality, communication responsiveness, corrective action speed, audit cooperation
💡 The Service dimension is the most overlooked
The exam tests the Service dimension because organizations frequently measure Quality, Cost, and Delivery while ignoring Service. A supplier who delivers conforming product on time at competitive cost — but takes 6 weeks to respond to SCARs and refuses audit requests — has a serious quality partnership problem that the first three dimensions won't reveal.
2
Practice Questions
A supplier scorecard shows: Quality = 99.2% conforming, Delivery = 97.8% on time, Cost = competitive. The quality manager nevertheless recommends placing this supplier on a watch list. Investigation reveals: average SCAR response time = 94 days (target: 30 days), 3 audit requests declined in the past year, zero completed corrective actions despite 7 quality notifications. Which of the four performance dimensions reveals this supplier's risk?
B is correct. The Service dimension captures the supplier's quality management partnership behaviors: corrective action responsiveness, audit cooperation, and communication quality. While current Quality and Delivery metrics look good, the absence of functioning corrective action processes means quality problems that DO occur will not be systematically eliminated. A supplier who refuses audits and ignores SCARs is signaling that quality management is not embedded in their culture — which predicts future quality failures that the current conformance rate doesn't yet reveal.
✦
From Bossert & Durivage — Supplier Scorecard Design

Sources: Bossert, J.L., Supplier Management Handbook, 6th ed., 2004; Durivage, M.A., The Certified Supplier Quality Professional Handbook, ASQ Quality Press, 2017

Scorecard dimensionKey metricsTypical weightMeasurement approach
QualityIncoming inspection pass rate; PPM defective; SCAR response time; SCAR recurrence rate; Cpk on critical characteristics40–50%Incoming inspection records; corrective action database; capability studies
DeliveryOn-time delivery rate; lead time consistency; fill rate; advance notification of delivery changes25–30%Purchase order receipt records; shipping notifications
ResponsivenessSCAR acknowledgment time; quality concern response time; engineering change incorporation speed; communication effectiveness15–20%SCAR database timestamps; quality team feedback ratings
CostPrice variance to contract; total cost of ownership including quality failures; cost reduction suggestions provided10–15%Purchase orders; quality cost attribution records
💡 Durivage — Scorecard as relationship tool, not just measurement
Durivage emphasizes that supplier scorecards serve two purposes beyond measurement: (1) Communication — sharing the scorecard regularly with supplier management makes expectations explicit and prevents the "we didn't know we had a problem" response to corrective actions; (2) Development platform — scorecard data identifies which supplier capabilities to invest in developing, prioritizing development resources on the supplier attributes most critical to performance. Suppliers who receive regular scorecard feedback and joint review meetings show significantly better performance improvement than those who only receive scorecards during problems.
A quality manager has been sharing supplier scorecards quarterly with all suppliers. She notices that Supplier X consistently scores 78/100 but never improves despite the scorecard. Investigation reveals: Supplier X receives the scorecard by email, files it, and never reviews it with quality management. Which corrective action best addresses the root cause of the scorecard's ineffectiveness?
D is correct. Durivage's principle: a supplier scorecard that is sent but not jointly reviewed is a measurement system without a feedback loop. Scorecard data becomes actionable only when supplier management engages with the data, understands the gaps, commits to specific improvement actions, and is held accountable for results in the next review. Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs) with joint scorecard review transform the scorecard from a report into a management dialogue. The agenda: review performance trends, identify root causes of below-target dimensions, agree on improvement actions with owners and timelines, follow up on previous commitments. This is the supplier management equivalent of a CAPA system — the scorecard identifies the problem; the QBR drives the solution.
✦
Supplier Scorecard — Visual Performance Dashboard

The CMQ/OE exam tests your ability to read supplier scorecard data and determine the appropriate management action. The radar chart below shows a typical multi-dimensional scorecard output.

💡 Reading the radar chart for exam questions
The radar chart makes multi-dimensional supplier performance visible at a glance. Key interpretations:

Large, balanced polygon → strong overall supplier; all dimensions above target
Elongated shape → strong in some dimensions, weak in others; not a balanced partner
Small polygon → consistently underperforming across dimensions; development plan or replacement required
One spike, narrow elsewhere → single-dimension strength that may mask systemic weaknesses

For the exam: Supplier A (green) has excellent delivery (95%) but weak responsiveness (62%) — a SCAR process issue. Supplier B (blue) has excellent responsiveness (90%) but weaker quality (74%) — a process capability issue. The question might ask: which supplier needs a corrective action request (Supplier A — responsiveness below threshold) vs. which needs a capability improvement plan (Supplier B — quality trend is the concern).
§VI · Topic 3
Supplier Risk Management
📚 BoK: VI.B
1
Key Supplier Risk Types
Risk typeDescriptionMitigation
Concentration/Single-source riskOne supplier provides 100% of a critical material — any disruption halts productionQualify alternative suppliers; build strategic safety stock; multi-source where possible
Financial stability riskSupplier may fail financially, disrupting supply or reducing quality investmentMonitor supplier financial health; qualify alternatives proactively; contractual protections
Quality riskSupplier quality system inadequate; nonconforming material entering productionSupplier audit; incoming inspection; qualification requirements; SCAR process
Geographic/Political riskNatural disasters, political instability, regulatory changes affecting supplyGeographic diversification; supply chain mapping; contingency stocking
💡 Financial stability is a quality risk — not just a procurement risk
Financially distressed suppliers reduce quality investments: deferred maintenance, reduced staff, cheaper materials, faster production at expense of quality. Green current metrics from a financially distressed supplier predict future quality deterioration. Proactive risk management identifies this BEFORE it becomes a quality problem.
2
Practice Questions
A quality manager learns that a key supplier is experiencing significant financial difficulty — late payments to their own suppliers, reduced workforce, and rumors of potential bankruptcy. The supplier's current quality metrics remain green: 99.1% conforming, 98% on-time delivery. A colleague says "no action needed — their metrics are fine." Which supply chain risk principle supports the quality manager's concern?
A is correct. The handbook's supplier risk management section identifies financial stability as a direct supply quality risk because financial distress reliably precedes quality deterioration. The sequence: financial pressure → deferred equipment maintenance → reduced quality staffing → cheaper material substitution → quality metric deterioration → supply disruption or failure. Quality managers who wait for metrics to deteriorate before acting will already be in a supply crisis when they finally respond. Proactive risk management monitors leading indicators — of which supplier financial health is one — and begins alternative qualification before the crisis materializes.
✦
From Durivage — Supply Chain Risk Categories

Source: Durivage, M.A., The Certified Supplier Quality Professional Handbook, ASQ Quality Press, 2017

Durivage identifies supply chain risk as multi-dimensional — each category requires different monitoring and mitigation strategies:

Risk categoryDescriptionMitigation strategy
Quality riskSupplier's processes produce nonconforming material; process capability below requirements; measurement system inadequateCapability studies before qualification; Gauge R&R verification; incoming inspection correlated to supplier process data
Supply continuity riskSingle-source dependency; supplier financial instability; geographic concentration (natural disaster, geopolitical)Dual sourcing for critical components; safety stock; business continuity planning with supplier
Sub-tier riskSupplier's own suppliers introduce quality or supply disruption risks that propagate up the supply chainSupply chain mapping to identify critical sub-tiers; flow-down of quality requirements through supplier contracts
Counterfeit material riskFraudulent or misrepresented materials entering the supply chain, particularly in electronics and aerospaceAuthorized distributor requirements; certificate of conformance verification; incoming inspection protocols for high-risk parts
Regulatory/compliance riskSupplier fails to meet applicable regulations (environmental, safety, labor) creating legal and reputational risk for the customerSupplier code of conduct requirements; social responsibility audits; regulatory compliance verification in approval process
💡 Durivage — Sub-tier risk is the hidden supply chain threat
Organizations typically have good visibility into their Tier 1 suppliers but limited visibility into Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers (their suppliers' suppliers). Major supply chain disruptions often originate at sub-tier level: a single-source Tier 2 component used by multiple Tier 1 suppliers simultaneously fails, creating a supply shortage across the entire industry simultaneously. Durivage recommends supply chain mapping: identify all sub-tier suppliers for critical materials and components, and apply risk management to the full chain, not just Tier 1 relationships.
✦
Supply Chain Risk Matrix — Heat Map

The risk matrix is the most common graphical format for supply chain risk questions on the CMQ/OE exam. You must be able to read the matrix, classify a risk by zone, and select the appropriate response strategy.

Risk scoreZoneManagement responseSupply chain example
16–25CriticalAvoid or immediately escalate — management action required; risk may justify not undertaking the activitySingle-source supplier for a safety-critical component with recent financial distress signals
12–15HighActive mitigation required — formal mitigation plan, owner assigned, tracked at management levelSingle-source supplier (reliable 3 years) for production-critical component — dual-source, safety stock, continuity plan
8–10MediumMonitor with mitigation plan — mitigation actions taken; periodic reviewKey supplier showing early delivery performance degradation — enhanced monitoring, proactive engagement
1–6LowAccept and monitor — no immediate action; include in periodic risk reviewMinor cosmetic variation in a non-critical component from a financially healthy multi-source supplier
⚠️ The low-likelihood high-impact exam trap
A risk with Likelihood=2 and Impact=5 scores 10 (Medium zone). The exam may present this as "low risk because the supplier has been reliable for 3 years." The correct answer: risk score is Medium-High regardless of history because a single occurrence of a high-impact event (production halt, safety issue) justifies active mitigation. The risk matrix evaluates consequence severity, not just probability. A low-probability catastrophic outcome requires a different response than a high-probability trivial outcome with the same mathematical risk score.
§VI · Topic 4
Supplier Communication & Improvement
📚 BoK: VI.C, VI.E
1
Supplier Communication Requirements

The handbook specifies that the customer organization must explicitly communicate quality requirements so suppliers know what is expected:

Communication elementFailure consequence
Specific quality requirements and specificationsSupplier manufactures to their own interpretation — misaligned with customer needs
Critical-to-quality dimensions and tolerancesSupplier optimizes for non-critical features while neglecting critical ones
Inspection and acceptance criteriaSupplier passes product that customer will reject — wasted production
Change notification requirementsSupplier makes process changes without notice — undetected quality impact
⚠️ Responsibility for communication is the CUSTOMER's
The handbook places the communication obligation on the customer organization. If you send a purchase order without quality specifications and the supplier delivers nonconforming material, the handbook points to the customer's failure to communicate — not the supplier's failure to guess what you wanted.
2
SCAR — Supplier Corrective Action Request
ComponentRequirement
ContainmentImmediate action to prevent further nonconforming material from entering production
Root cause analysisVerified root cause — not assumed. "Operator retrained" is containment at best, not root cause analysis.
Corrective actionSystemic action that eliminates the verified root cause
Effectiveness verificationEvidence that the corrective action has eliminated the root cause and prevented recurrence
3
Practice Questions
A supplier responds to a SCAR with: "We have retrained our operators on the dimensional inspection procedure. This issue will not recur." The quality manager rejects this response. Which SCAR principle supports her rejection?
B is correct. A complete SCAR response requires: (1) verified root cause analysis — not an assumption, (2) corrective action that addresses that specific verified root cause, and (3) effectiveness verification showing the problem was eliminated. "Operator retrained" assumes the root cause is operator knowledge. Without root cause analysis confirming this assumption, the training may be solving a non-existent root cause while the real cause (equipment tolerance drift, ambiguous specification, measurement system error) continues to produce defects. The quality manager correctly requires documented root cause analysis before accepting the corrective action claim.
3
Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR) Process

The SCAR is the formal communication mechanism when a supplier nonconformance requires corrective action. The handbook describes both the process and the escalation path:

SCAR StageActivityTypical timeline
IssueCustomer sends formal SCAR to supplier documenting the nonconformance, quantity affected, and requested responseWithin 24-48 hours of identifying the nonconformance
ContainmentSupplier confirms immediate containment: sorting affected inventory, holding shipments, notifying customer of material in transit24-72 hours response required
Root Cause AnalysisSupplier investigates and identifies verified root cause (not just "operator error")5-15 business days depending on complexity
Corrective Action PlanSupplier proposes specific actions to eliminate root cause and prevent recurrence; includes implementation timeline and responsible ownerSubmitted with or shortly after RCA
VerificationCustomer reviews the plan; supplier implements; customer verifies effectiveness through incoming inspection data or audit30-90 days post-implementation
CloseCustomer formally closes SCAR when effectiveness is verifiedAfter evidence confirms the corrective action worked
💡 SCAR escalation path
When a supplier fails to respond to SCARs adequately or repeatedly:
Level 1: Issue SCAR → expect 24-hour containment acknowledgment
Level 2: Escalate to supplier management if response inadequate
Level 3: Customer executive contact to supplier executive
Level 4: Increased incoming inspection (move from ship-to-stock back to 100% inspection)
Level 5: Supplier development audit — customer quality engineers work at supplier site
Level 6: Suspend new business; begin qualifying alternative supplier
Level 7: Decertify and remove from approved supplier list
4
Additional Practice Questions
A quality manager receives a SCAR response from a supplier: "Root cause: Incoming material did not meet specification. Corrective action: We have notified our raw material supplier to improve quality." The quality manager rejects this SCAR response. What are the two problems with this response?
B is correct. Two critical SCAR response failures: (1) SHALLOW ROOT CAUSE: "Incoming material didn't meet spec" identifies the contributing condition but not the system failure. The real root cause is: why did the supplier's incoming inspection process fail to detect the out-of-spec material? What is the incoming inspection procedure? What went wrong in it? The corrective action must address the inspection process failure, not just the material condition. (2) UNVERIFIABLE CORRECTIVE ACTION: "Notifying our supplier" is a communication activity, not a corrective action. A proper corrective action would specify: what the sub-supplier must change (process? specification? inspection method?), when, verified by what evidence, and how the quality manager will confirm effectiveness. The quality manager must reject and require a complete 8D or equivalent root cause analysis with verifiable corrective actions.
✦
SCAR Process — Supplier Corrective Action Flow

The SCAR (Supplier Corrective Action Request) is the primary supplier quality communication tool. Know the 6 stages, the customer and supplier responsibilities at each stage, and the escalation trigger.

§VI · Topic 5
Supplier Certification
📚 BoK: VI.F
1
Supplier Certification — Purpose and Benefit

Supplier certification is the process of formally recognizing a supplier who has demonstrated consistent quality performance meeting defined criteria.

AspectDescription
Primary quality benefitQualified suppliers may be authorized to ship materials directly to stock without incoming inspection — reducing cost and improving flow
Requirement for certificationDemonstrated consistent conforming quality performance over a defined period — earned, not assumed
Does certification eliminate audits?No — ongoing monitoring continues; certification reflects current performance, not permanent unconditional trust
Partnerships (highest level)True supplier partnerships involve open information sharing, joint quality improvement, and mutual investment in each other's success
2
Practice Questions
A quality manager wants to implement a ship-to-stock program for three suppliers. Which prerequisite must be established before ship-to-stock can be implemented?
B is correct. Ship-to-stock means materials bypass incoming inspection and go directly to production or inventory. The quality prerequisite: the supplier must have demonstrated sufficient, consistent quality performance that incoming inspection is no longer necessary as a verification step. This is the logic of supplier certification — you invest in verifying the supplier's quality system so you can reduce or eliminate costly incoming inspection on their materials. A supplier without a demonstrated conforming quality record cannot be approved for ship-to-stock regardless of other IT or logistics factors.
✦
Supplier Approval Stages — Certification Ladder
§VI · Topic 6
Logistics & Material Acceptance
📚 BoK: VI.G
1
Incoming Material Inspection Strategy
ApproachWhen appropriateQuality principle
100% inspectionNew supplier; high-risk material; history of quality issues; critical safety componentsMaximum protection but costly and non-value-adding; target for elimination through supplier development
Sampling inspectionEstablished supplier with some history; risk-based judgmentStatistically based detection; AQL sampling plans; balances cost and risk
Skip-lot inspectionSupplier with consistently good performance; as a transition to certificationReward for good performance; maintains some detection capability while reducing cost
Ship-to-stock (no inspection)Certified supplier with demonstrated consistently conforming qualityPrevention has replaced detection; supplier quality system assurance replaces incoming inspection
💡 The inspection strategy principle
The handbook's preferred direction: move progressively from 100% inspection → sampling → skip-lot → ship-to-stock as supplier quality is verified and improved. Incoming inspection is a detection control — the goal of supplier development is to make it unnecessary through prevention (supplier capability improvement).
2
Practice Questions
A quality manager reviews her inspection program and finds: 3 suppliers account for 87% of all incoming quality escapes; 12 suppliers have had zero escapes in 24 months. She redesigns her inspection program accordingly. Which supply chain quality management principle does her redesign best represent?
A is correct. The risk-based inspection principle: allocate inspection resources where the risk is highest and reduce them where performance is proven. The 3 suppliers generating 87% of escapes need intensive incoming inspection, supplier corrective actions, and supplier development resources. The 12 suppliers with zero escapes in 24 months are candidates for skip-lot inspection or ship-to-stock certification — applying the same inspection intensity to them wastes resources that should be focused on the high-risk suppliers. This is Pareto principle (vital few = 3 suppliers, useful many = 12) applied to incoming inspection resource allocation.
✦
Supply Chain Logistics — Quality Touchpoints
§VII · Training & Development
Section VII Overview

Training and development ensures employees have the competencies to execute quality objectives. The exam tests: training plans aligned with strategy, TNA methods, adult learning principles, delivery methods, Kirkpatrick 4 levels, and Phillips ROI.

📋 Exam weight: 16 questions (~10%)
📚 BoK: VII.A through VII.D
🧮 Calculation: Phillips ROI formula
Topics
Training Plans — strategic alignment, ADDIE model, leadership development, PDPs
Training Needs Analysis — gap analysis, deficiency analysis, survey methods
Training Design & Delivery — methods comparison, blended learning
Adult Learning Principles — Knowles andragogy, problem-centered orientation
Kirkpatrick 4 Levels — Reaction, Learning, Behavior, Results; Level 2-3 gap
Training ROI — Phillips formula, BCR distinction, worked calculation
§VII · Topic 2
Training Needs Analysis (TNA)

TNA identifies WHAT training is needed, WHO needs it, and WHY. The exam tests TNA tools, gap analysis, and the deficiency analysis principle that training only solves skill/knowledge gaps — not motivation or process problems.

📚 BoK: VII.B
⚠️ Key trap: Training is not the solution to every performance problem
1
TNA Tools
MethodWhat it revealsBest for
Performance gap analysisDifference between current and required performanceIdentifying specific skill/knowledge deficiencies in defined roles
SurveysBroad assessment of perceived training needs across many employeesInitial scanning of priorities across large populations
Performance reviewsIndividual performance gaps documented by managersRole-specific, person-specific skill deficiency identification
Regulatory guidance reviewMandatory training requirements from regulations and standardsCompliance training needs — non-discretionary requirements
Observation and interviewsActual work behavior vs. required behaviorOperational needs that documentation doesn't capture
2
Deficiency Analysis — Critical Pre-Training Question
⚠️ Training only solves skill and knowledge deficiencies
Training CAN solve: Doesn't know HOW to use SPC software; new hire doesn't know quality procedures; operator hasn't been shown how to calibrate the gauge

Training CANNOT solve: Employee knows how but is unmotivated (motivation problem); knows how but process design prevents it (process problem); has the skills but lacks the tools (resource problem)

If the cause is a skill/knowledge gap → training. If the cause is motivation, process, or resources → a different intervention is needed.
3
Practice Questions
Operators consistently use the wrong calibration reference standard despite training records showing 100% completion and 85%+ post-training test scores. Investigation reveals the correct reference standard is locked in a cabinet requiring supervisor approval to access, and supervisors are often unavailable during calibration windows. What intervention is needed?
C is correct. The deficiency analysis reveals: knowledge acquired (training done), competency confirmed (85%+ scores). The performance failure is caused by a resource access barrier — not a training gap. Training cannot fix this. The solution: change the storage policy or redesign the calibration window timing.
✦
From Mitchell — Performance Gap Analysis

Source: Mitchell, G., The Trainer's Handbook, 3rd ed., AMACOM, 1998

Mitchell presents the performance gap model as the analytical foundation of TNA — a systematic process to determine whether training is actually the right intervention:

Performance gap analysis stepQuestion answeredPossible finding
1. Define required performanceWhat specific behaviors must the person demonstrate to perform the job effectively?"Quality engineers must be able to independently conduct a Gauge R&R study and interpret results" — specific and behavioral
2. Describe actual performanceWhat is the person currently doing? How does it differ from required performance?"Quality engineers collect measurements but cannot analyze GRR results without assistance from the quality manager"
3. Define the gapWhat specific performance deficit exists between required and actual?Gap: "Cannot independently calculate %GRR, identify whether it passes/fails, or determine whether repeatability or reproducibility is the dominant issue"
4. Identify the causeWHY does the gap exist? Is it a skill/knowledge issue (training can fix) or something else (training cannot fix)?Cause A: "Engineers were never trained on GRR calculation" → Training solution. Cause B: "Engineers know how but don't have access to the required software" → Resource solution, not training
5. Select the interventionTraining only if cause = skill/knowledge gap. Otherwise: resources, incentives, process redesign, job aids, etc.Training if cause is knowledge. Software procurement if cause is access. Manager coaching if cause is confidence. Job aid if cause is rare task requiring memory.
⚠️ Mitchell's most important TNA principle
"Training is not the solution to every performance problem. In fact, if training is the only solution you consider, you will frequently prescribe the wrong intervention." Mitchell identifies that approximately 80% of performance problems have non-training root causes. The TNA's most critical contribution is determining WHEN NOT to train — saving training investment for the 20% of problems where knowledge or skill is genuinely the root cause.
✦
Performance Gap Model — Visual Diagram

The performance gap model is the diagnostic foundation of every training needs analysis. The CMQ/OE exam tests your ability to identify the gap, determine its cause, and select the correct intervention — which is NOT always training.

Performance gap causeInterventionWhat training will NOT fix
Skill/Knowledge deficit — employee does not know HOW to performTraining — the only gap that training actually addressesN/A — this is what training is for
Environmental barrier — employee knows how but the work environment prevents correct performanceProcess redesign, remove the barrier, improve tools/equipmentTraining an employee to use a broken tool correctly does not fix the broken tool
Resource deficit — employee lacks the tools, materials, or time to perform correctlyProvide the resources — software, equipment, time allocationTraining employees who lack a required software licence does not give them the software
Incentive misalignment — employee knows how but is not motivated/rewarded to perform correctlyIncentive redesign, performance management, clear expectationsTraining does not change the incentive structure; employees will revert to what is measured and rewarded
Clarity deficit — employee is uncertain what standard is expectedClarify expectations, set clear standards, communicate performance requirementsTraining on technique when the real issue is unclear expectations about what "good" looks like
§VII · Topic 3
Training Design & Delivery
📚 BoK: VII.C
1
Delivery Methods
MethodPrimary advantagePrimary limitation
Classroom / instructor-ledInteractive; allows questions; good for complex conceptsRequires travel/coordination; fixed schedule; expensive for small groups
On-the-job training (OJT)Highest task fidelity — real equipment, real contextInconsistent quality; can embed bad habits; may disrupt production
SimulationRealistic practice without real-world consequencesDevelopment cost; may not replicate all real-world variables
Computer-based / e-learningSelf-paced; scalable for distributed workforce; consistent deliveryLimited interactivity; poor for hands-on skills; requires technology
Coaching and mentoringIndividualized; builds on specific person's needsTime-intensive; quality depends on coach capability
2
Practice Questions
A quality director needs to train 150 quality technicians on a new SPC software system. The technicians are located across 8 global production sites. The system has a complex interface requiring practice to master. Which delivery approach is most appropriate?
A is correct. The multi-site global distribution makes central classroom training impractical. Computer-based modules address geographic distribution with consistent content. But a complex interface requires hands-on practice that CBT alone cannot develop — simulation or supervised practice sessions provide this. Blended approach: CBT for knowledge + simulation/practice for skill development.
✦
From Mitchell — Writing Measurable Learning Objectives

Source: Mitchell, G., The Trainer's Handbook: The AMA Guide to Effective Training, 3rd ed., AMACOM, 1998

Mitchell presents the behavioural objectives framework — the foundation of training design that connects TNA to delivery to Kirkpatrick evaluation. A complete learning objective has three components:

Objective componentDefinitionQuality training example
Performance (Action verb)What the learner will be ABLE TO DO after training — must be observable and measurable; use action verbs (calculate, identify, construct, demonstrate, apply)"Calculate Cpk from process data" — NOT "understand process capability" (not measurable)
ConditionThe circumstances under which the performance will occur — what resources/constraints apply"Given a data set of 25 measurements and the specification limits..."
Standard (Criterion)The acceptable level of performance — how well must the learner perform to demonstrate competency"...correctly calculate Cpk within ±0.05 of the true value in under 5 minutes"
💡 Complete objective example
Poor objective: "Participants will understand statistical process control" — passive, unmeasurable, no condition, no standard

Mitchell's well-formed objective: "Given a 25-point X̄-R control chart with annotated Western Electric violations, participants will correctly identify all out-of-control signals and state the appropriate investigation response for each signal type, with 100% accuracy on signals 1, 4, and 5 and 85% accuracy on signals 2, 3, and 6."

Why this matters for the CMQ/OE exam: well-written objectives (1) define exactly what Level 2 (Kirkpatrick) evaluation must test, (2) specify the job performance that Level 3 evaluation must observe, and (3) make it possible to measure Level 4 results by connecting training to specific on-the-job quality outcomes.
A training manager writes this learning objective for a DMAIC training program: "Participants will learn DMAIC and be able to use it." A training designer says this objective is inadequate. What specifically is wrong with it, and how should it be revised?
C is correct. Mitchell's three-component framework: Performance (observable action verb) + Condition (circumstances) + Standard (acceptable level). "Learn" is a mental state, not an observable performance — you cannot observe someone "learning." "Use it" is too vague — use it to do what, under what conditions, at what quality level? Without all three components, there is no basis for Level 2 evaluation (what test would you write to assess whether "learn DMAIC" was achieved?) and no connection to Level 3 (what specific behavior would you observe to confirm "able to use DMAIC"?). The revised objective provides all three: performance (complete Define and Measure phases), condition (given a defined quality problem with baseline data), standard (meeting project charter checklist criteria in 4 hours).
✦
From Mitchell — Selecting Training Delivery Methods
MethodBest for (Mitchell)Avoid when
Lecture/presentationContent transfer of information and concepts to large groups; new regulatory requirements that everyone must knowSkills development — lecture describes skills but cannot build them; when active participation improves retention
Case studyApplying concepts to realistic scenarios; developing analytical judgment; learning from others' experiences without the cost of direct experienceLearners lack foundational knowledge — case study analysis requires a conceptual framework to apply to the case
Role play / simulationPracticing interpersonal skills (conflict resolution, audit communication, coaching); building skills that require feedback from another person; high-stakes situations where live practice is too riskyKnowledge-only objectives — role play is overkill for information transfer
On-the-job training (OJT)Skills that are highly job-specific and difficult to simulate; when a coach/mentor is available; transferring tacit knowledge from expert to noviceSafety-critical situations where errors have real consequences; when quality of instruction is inconsistent between OJT coaches
Self-directed / e-learningDistributed workforces needing consistent content delivery; topics where learners have different knowledge starting points; refresher training for experienced personnelComplex skills requiring human interaction and real-time feedback; team-based problem-solving development
✦
ADDIE Model — Instructional Design Cycle

ADDIE is the foundational instructional design model tested in §VII. The diagram below shows both the sequential flow AND the iterative nature — evaluation feeds back into all phases.

PhaseKey activitiesCritical outputCommon failure
AnalysisConduct TNA; confirm performance gap; identify target audience characteristics; determine if training is the right solution; analyse learning constraints (budget, time, technology)Needs analysis report confirming: (1) a performance gap exists, (2) training can close it, (3) target audience definedSkipping TNA and designing training for a problem that training cannot solve — producing expensive courses that don't improve performance
DesignWrite measurable learning objectives (Performance + Condition + Standard); sequence content; select delivery methods; plan assessment instruments for each Kirkpatrick level; define success criteriaCourse blueprint with objectives, content sequence, delivery method, and evaluation plan — approved before development beginsSkipping evaluation design — deciding how to measure Kirkpatrick L3 and L4 after the training runs, when it is too late to collect baseline data
DevelopCreate training materials (slides, workbooks, exercises, e-learning modules, job aids); pilot test with representative sample; revise based on pilot feedbackFinished, piloted training materials ready for deliveryNo pilot test — delivering untested training to full audience; defects discovered during live delivery are expensive and damage credibility
ImplementDeliver training; manage logistics; facilitate learning; support learners; collect Level 1 reaction data immediatelyCompleted training event; Level 1 data collectedDelivery without manager communication — learners return to work without their manager understanding what was trained or what behaviour change is expected
EvaluateMeasure L1 reaction, L2 learning, L3 behaviour (30–90 days), L4 results (3–12 months); compare to objectives; report to stakeholders; update design for future iterationsEvaluation report showing training effectiveness at all feasible Kirkpatrick levels; recommendations for improvementStopping at Level 1 — reporting satisfaction scores to leadership as proof of effectiveness without measuring learning transfer or business impact
✦
Bloom's Taxonomy — Cognitive Levels in Training Design

Bloom's Taxonomy defines six levels of cognitive learning. The CMQ/OE exam tests at primarily the Application and Analysis levels — memorisation is not enough. When designing quality training, the learning objective level must match the job performance level required.

Figure 8: Bloom's Taxonomy — quality training objectives should target Apply level and above

💡 Bloom's level determines the assessment method
Remember/Understand: Multiple choice, true/false, fill-in-the-blank — tests whether the learner knows the concept
Apply: Worked problems, case studies, simulations — tests whether the learner can use the concept in a new situation
Analyse: Case analyses, root cause exercises — tests whether the learner can break down a complex situation
Evaluate/Create: Project work, design exercises, peer critique — tests whether the learner can make quality judgements and produce new work

Most quality training failures happen when objectives are written at the Remember level ("participants will understand Cpk") but the job requires Apply level ("participants will calculate Cpk from production data and decide whether to continue or stop production"). The mismatch produces graduates who can define Cpk but cannot use it.
§VII · Topic 4
Adult Learning Principles (Andragogy)
📚 BoK: VII.C
1
Knowles' Five Principles
PrincipleQuality training design implication
Self-directedGive learners some control over pace and approach
Experience as resourceConnect new content to what learners already know from their work
Readiness to learnTime training to actual need — when learners need it, they are ready
Problem-centered orientationUse real quality problems from their actual work as learning scenarios
Internal motivationMost effectively motivated by career advancement and professional competence, not just external rewards
💡 Problem-centered — most tested for quality training
Quality training using learners' own production data and real workplace problems is far more effective than generic examples. Technicians seeing their own process's actual data in control chart training immediately understand relevance. This principle explains WHY quality training must be contextualized.
2
Practice Questions
A quality manager is designing SPC training for production supervisors. She can use (A) a standard SPC textbook curriculum with generic examples, or (B) a curriculum built around the supervisors' own production line data with specific defect problems they are currently facing. Which aligns better with adult learning principles?
C is correct. Knowles' problem-centered orientation: adults learn most effectively when training is organized around real problems they currently face. Using supervisors' own production line data: connects to prior experience (experience as resource), creates immediate relevance and readiness, allows practice on real problems they actually need to solve. Learning transfer is maximized when training context matches work context.
✦
Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle

Kolb's model is the most tested adult learning theory diagram in the CMQ/OE exam. Know all four stages, the two learning dimensions, and how the four learning styles relate to the cycle.

Kolb stageAdult learning activityQuality training exampleAssociated style
Concrete Experience (CE)Doing something — having a direct experience with the content; hands-on practiceParticipants run an actual control chart on live production data during the workshopAccommodator (AE+CE): learns by doing and experimenting; prefers trial and error
Reflective Observation (RO)Observing and reflecting — watching what happened; reviewing the experience; examining from multiple perspectivesDebriefing session: "What did you notice when the control chart showed a special cause? What did you feel uncertain about?"Diverger (CE+RO): imaginative; generates ideas; prefers brainstorming; strong in arts and people skills
Abstract Conceptualisation (AC)Theorising — drawing conclusions from the reflection; developing rules and principles; conceptual understandingLecture/explanation: "The Western Electric rules define what constitutes non-random variation — here is why the 8-point run rule works statistically"Assimilator (RO+AC): logical; systematic; prefers reading and lectures; strong in science and information
Active Experimentation (AE)Planning and trying — applying the new concept to a new situation; testing understanding through actionApplication exercise: "Here is a new dataset from a different process — identify all Western Electric violations and determine appropriate response"Converger (AC+AE): practical problem-solver; prefers technical tasks and experiments; finds single correct answers
💡 Malcolm Knowles — Andragogy: 6 principles of adult learning
Knowles identified that adults learn differently from children. His andragogy principles directly inform quality training design:

1. Self-concept — adults need to know WHY they are learning something before they will engage; open with the business case for the training
2. Experience — adults bring rich prior experience; build on it (acknowledge what they already know before introducing new concepts)
3. Readiness to learn — adults learn best when the content solves a current, real problem they face; connect training to participants' actual work situations
4. Learning orientation — adults are life/task-oriented, not subject-oriented; they want to know how to DO something, not just understand a concept
5. Motivation — adults are primarily motivated by internal factors (career growth, problem-solving ability) rather than external grades or certificates
6. Need to know — adults want to understand how the learning is relevant to them before investing attention in it
A quality trainer designs a 1-day SPC workshop using only lectures and slides. Post-training assessment shows 85% knowledge test scores. However, four months later, operators are still not responding correctly to control chart signals. Applying Kolb's learning cycle, what is missing from the training design?
A is correct. Kolb's principle: learning requires all four cycle stages for full transfer to behaviour. Lecture-only training activates only Abstract Conceptualisation (understanding the theory of Western Electric rules). It skips: Concrete Experience (actually working a real control chart), Reflective Observation (examining what happened when a signal appeared and how it felt to respond), and Active Experimentation (practising the response decision on new, unfamiliar data). Operators who have only heard about control chart response may understand it conceptually (hence 85% test score) but have no behavioural pattern to activate when facing a real chart in production. The fix: add simulation exercises (CE), structured reflection (RO), and practice on new data sets (AE) to complete the learning cycle before operators return to the floor.
§VII · Topic 5
Kirkpatrick's 4 Levels of Training Evaluation
📚 BoK: VII.D
⚠️ Trap risk: Very High — Level 2 pass ≠ Level 3 application
1
The Four Levels
LevelNameWhat it measuresHow measured
1ReactionDid participants like the training?Post-training satisfaction surveys
2LearningDid participants learn?Post-training tests, skills demonstrations
3BehaviorAre participants applying what they learned?Observation, supervisor assessment (weeks/months after)
4ResultsDid organizational performance improve?Quality metrics, defect rates, cost reduction — before vs. after
⚠️ The Level 2-3 gap — most tested failure
Training participants pass Level 2 (90% test score) but 6 months later nobody applies the skills (Level 3 failure). This occurs when the WORK ENVIRONMENT doesn't support application: supervisors don't reinforce, systems aren't available, old behaviors are still rewarded. The training succeeded; the transfer system failed. Solution: supervisor commitment, system changes, and accountability — not more training.
⚠️ Level 4 for CFO justification
A CFO makes resource allocation decisions based on organizational return. Level 1 (satisfaction) and Level 2 (learning) data are irrelevant to a CFO. Level 4 (results) — quality improvements, cost reductions attributable to training — is the only data that justifies continued training investment in financial terms.
2
Practice Questions
A DMAIC training program produced 91% average test scores (Level 2). Eight months later, only 2 of 12 trained engineers have applied DMAIC on actual projects; the other 10 returned to ad-hoc problem-solving despite knowing DMAIC. Which Kirkpatrick level reveals this gap and what is the likely cause?
B is correct. Level 2 data (91% scores) confirms learning. The gap is between knowing DMAIC (Level 2) and applying it (Level 3 not achieved). Environmental causes: managers didn't assign DMAIC projects, ad-hoc problem-solving is faster under production pressure and continues to be implicitly rewarded, no accountability for applying the methodology. Intervention: create DMAIC project assignments, establish manager expectations, make DMAIC application a performance expectation.
3
The Level 2-3 Transfer Gap — In Depth
💡 Why Level 2 success does NOT guarantee Level 3 application
People who demonstrate knowledge after training (Level 2) often fail to apply it on the job (Level 3). This is called the transfer gap and it is caused by the WORK ENVIRONMENT, not the training itself. Common transfer gap causes:

• No opportunity to apply: Trained on DMAIC but no DMAIC projects are assigned
• Manager doesn't reinforce: Supervisor never asks about or supports new skills application
• Old behaviors still rewarded: Ad-hoc problem-solving still gets praised; new structured approach is slower initially
• Peer pressure to revert: Team culture pulls individuals back to old methods
• Systems don't support new behavior: Trained to use new quality software but still asked to use the old spreadsheet

Intervention required: The transfer gap is a management/system problem — not a training problem. More training will not fix it. Required: supervisor commitment, accountability systems, assigned practice opportunities, and removal of environmental barriers.
4
Matching Kirkpatrick Level to Stakeholder Need
StakeholderRelevant Kirkpatrick levelWhat they want to know
Training participantsLevel 1 (Reaction)Was the training useful, relevant, and well-delivered?
Training designer/facilitatorLevel 1 & 2Did people enjoy it? Did they learn? How can the program be improved?
Operations managerLevel 3 (Behavior)Are my people using the skills? Is daily work changing?
Quality director / executive teamLevel 4 (Results)Did quality metrics improve? Is the investment working?
CFO / FinanceLevel 4 + ROIWhat was the financial return on the training investment? Expressed as %ROI.
5
Additional Practice Questions
After Six Sigma Black Belt training, a quality director presents Level 1 data (95% satisfaction) and Level 2 data (89% post-test pass rate) to the CFO to justify continuing the program. The CFO responds: "This data tells me participants liked the training and passed a test. What I need to know is whether our quality costs went down and by how much." Which Kirkpatrick level is the CFO asking for, and why are Levels 1 and 2 insufficient for his decision?
B is correct. The CFO's question — "did our quality costs go down?" — is a Level 4 (Results) question. Level 1 (satisfaction) and Level 2 (learning) are insufficient for financial resource allocation decisions because: (1) a training program can be well-liked and knowledge-tested without ever producing organizational improvement, and (2) the CFO's responsibility is to allocate capital to investments that generate returns — which requires Level 4 outcome data or ROI calculations. The quality director must present: projects completed, COPQ reduction achieved, comparison to training investment cost. This is the Phillips ROI level: financial return attributable to training = the only language that justifies budget decisions in financial terms.
📚 Additional Reference: Mitchell, The Trainer's Handbook
Mitchell provides practical application of Kirkpatrick that complements the handbook theory. Key additions: designing Level 2 assessments that actually predict Level 3 transfer; building Level 4 measurement plans before training begins; creating learning contracts to improve behavioral application. For the exam, know the four levels from the handbook — use Mitchell's practical guidance in your day-to-day training management role.
✦
The Kirkpatrick 4-Level Model — Pyramid Diagram

The Kirkpatrick pyramid is one of the highest-frequency §VII diagrams on the CMQ/OE exam. Know each level's definition, who needs it, and what instrument measures it.

Figure 6: Kirkpatrick 4-Level Model — evaluation becomes harder and more valuable as you move up

LevelQuestion answeredMeasurement toolWho needs this dataLimitation
L1 — ReactionDid participants like the training? Were they satisfied with the experience?"Smile sheets" — end-of-course satisfaction surveys; typically 5-point rating scalesTraining department — to improve course design and deliveryHigh satisfaction does NOT predict learning or behaviour change; participants can love a course and learn nothing applicable
L2 — LearningDid participants acquire the intended knowledge, skills, or attitudes?Pre/post knowledge tests; skill demonstrations; simulation exercises; certification assessmentsTraining manager — to verify training effectiveness; trainer — to identify gapsHigh test scores do NOT guarantee job application — participants may know the correct answer on a test but not transfer the skill to work
L3 — BehaviourDid participants apply what they learned back on the job?Supervisor observation checklists (30/60/90 days post-training); 360-degree feedback; process audits; performance reviewsDirect manager — has the employee's performance actually changed?Requires time delay (cannot measure immediately); behaviour may not transfer without management support and reinforcement
L4 — ResultsDid the training produce the intended business outcome?KPI tracking (defect rate, scrap, customer complaints, cycle time); ROI calculation (Phillips model adds Level 5 — ROI %)Senior leadership / CFO — justifies training investment; connects training to strategyMost difficult to isolate — other factors (process changes, staffing, market conditions) may also affect the business KPI
⚠️ The Level 2 → Level 3 gap — the most tested Kirkpatrick concept
Participants can score 95% on a Level 2 knowledge test and still show zero behaviour change at Level 3. This transfer gap is the central challenge of training evaluation. Mitchell identifies the causes of the L2→L3 gap:

• Environmental barriers — manager does not reinforce the new behaviour; the work environment does not support the new approach
• No practice opportunity — the new skill is needed rarely; participants forget before they have a chance to apply
• Lack of confidence — participants understand the concept but feel uncertain applying it independently
• Culture resistance — "we don't do it that way here" overrides training content

The quality manager's response: design training with transfer in mind from the start — include manager briefings, on-the-job practice assignments, and 30/60-day follow-up check-ins. Evaluation planning begins during training design, not after delivery.
A quality training manager delivers a 2-day FMEA workshop. End-of-course surveys show average 4.6/5 satisfaction. Post-course tests show 89% knowledge retention. Six months later, a quality audit finds that product development teams are still not conducting FMEAs consistently. At which Kirkpatrick level has the training failed, and what is the most likely root cause?
B is correct. This is a classic Level 2 → Level 3 transfer gap. High L1 (satisfaction) and L2 (knowledge) scores confirm the training content was well-delivered and understood. The failure is at L3 — behaviour on the job. The most common cause of L3 failure after successful L2: the work environment does not support the new behaviour. FMEA will not be consistently conducted unless: (1) management explicitly requires it as part of the product development process, (2) a process exists to document and review FMEAs, (3) teams are held accountable for FMEA quality. Without environmental support, even perfectly designed and delivered training fails at transfer. The fix: manager briefing before training explaining the expectation; process update requiring FMEA documentation in product development; 60-day follow-up audit checking FMEA compliance.
§VII · Topic 6
Training ROI (Phillips Formula)
📚 BoK: VII.D
🧮 Formula: ROI (%) = (Net Benefits / Costs) × 100
1
Phillips ROI Formula
📐 FORMULA
ROI (%) = ((Benefits − Costs) / Costs) × 100

Or: ROI (%) = (Net Benefits / Program Costs) × 100

Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) = Total Benefits / Costs

Key: ROI uses NET benefits (benefits minus costs) in numerator. BCR uses TOTAL benefits. ROI of 100% = BCR of 2.0.
2
Practice Questions
CALCULATION: A quality improvement training program costs $250,000. Level 4 evaluation attributes: scrap reduction = $180,000/year; warranty cost reduction = $220,000/year; customer complaint handling reduction = $50,000/year. Calculate the ROI.
A is correct. Total benefits = $180K + $220K + $50K = $450,000. Net benefits = $450,000 − $250,000 = $200,000. ROI = ($200,000 / $250,000) × 100 = 80%. Note: Option A (180%) gives the BCR-based calculation, not the ROI. BCR = $450K/$250K = 1.8 = 180% if expressed that way, but the BCR formula is Total Benefits/Costs = 1.8 (not a percentage). ROI uses NET benefits: (Benefits−Costs)/Costs. Always subtract costs before dividing when calculating Phillips ROI.
3
BCR vs. ROI — The Critical Distinction
Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR)ROI (%)
FormulaBCR = Total Benefits / Program CostsROI = (Net Benefits / Program Costs) × 100 = ((Benefits − Costs) / Costs) × 100
NumeratorTOTAL benefits (before subtracting costs)NET benefits (benefits MINUS costs)
InterpretationBCR = 2.5 means $2.50 returned for every $1 investedROI = 150% means 150% return on the investment (net gain = 1.5× the cost)
RelationshipBCR = (ROI/100) + 1ROI = (BCR − 1) × 100
ExampleCosts = $100K, Benefits = $250K → BCR = 2.5Same data → ROI = (250-100)/100 × 100 = 150%
4
Additional Practice Questions
CALCULATION: A Lean manufacturing training program costs $180,000. Level 4 evaluation attributes the following quality improvements in the 12 months following training: WIP reduction (freed working capital) = $85,000 value; scrap reduction = $62,000/year; rework labor reduction = $48,000/year; customer complaint reduction (estimated cost avoided) = $35,000/year. Calculate: (a) Total annual benefits, (b) ROI, (c) BCR. Would you approve continued investment in this program?
C is correct. Calculations: Total benefits = $85K + $62K + $48K + $35K = $230,000. ROI = (($230,000 − $180,000) / $180,000) × 100 = ($50,000 / $180,000) × 100 = 27.8%. BCR = $230,000 / $180,000 = 1.28. At first glance, 27.8% ROI looks modest — but the critical analysis note: the $180K is a one-time training investment. The scrap reduction ($62K), rework reduction ($48K), and complaint reduction ($35K) are RECURRING annual savings. Year 2 net benefit = $145K with $0 additional training cost. Year 3 = another $145K. 3-year cumulative: Benefits $230K + $145K + $145K = $520K vs. $180K cost = 3-year ROI of 189%. The WIP reduction ($85K) is a one-time value. This analysis shows the training investment is strong on a multi-year basis even though the first-year-only ROI looks low.
A quality training manager presents her annual training ROI report showing: 47 training programs delivered, average Level 1 score = 4.2/5.0, Level 2 average = 84% pass rate, BCR = 2.1 based on Level 4 quality improvements. The CFO is satisfied. The training manager's supervisor asks: "What is the ROI?" She responds: "BCR of 2.1 is the same as ROI of 110%." Is she correct?
D is correct. The conversion: BCR = Total Benefits / Costs. ROI = Net Benefits / Costs = (Benefits − Costs) / Costs = Benefits/Costs − 1 = BCR − 1. Therefore ROI (as decimal) = BCR − 1, and ROI (%) = (BCR − 1) × 100. For BCR = 2.1: ROI = (2.1 − 1) × 100 = 110%. Verification: if Benefits = $210K and Costs = $100K, BCR = 210/100 = 2.1 ✓. ROI = (210-100)/100 × 100 = 110% ✓. The training manager correctly stated ROI of 110% from BCR of 2.1. Common trap: mistaking BCR for ROI (claiming BCR=2.1 means "210% ROI" — this would be true if ROI = BCR×100, but that formula is wrong).
✦
Phillips ROI Model — 5-Level Evaluation Chain

Jack Phillips extended Kirkpatrick's 4 levels by adding Level 5 — Return on Investment (ROI%). Know the complete chain, the ROI calculation formula, and the BCR vs. ROI distinction — these are the most calculation-tested items in §VII.

CALCULATION: A quality training programme costs $80,000 to design and deliver. Over 12 months, the programme produces measurable benefits: scrap reduction saves $85,000, rework reduction saves $60,000, and warranty claims reduction saves $35,000. Total measured benefits = $180,000. Calculate the ROI (%) and BCR, then select the correct interpretation.
D is correct. The critical distinction: ROI uses NET benefits (total benefits MINUS costs, then divide by costs); BCR uses TOTAL (gross) benefits divided by costs. Step-by-step: ROI = (Total Benefits − Programme Cost) ÷ Programme Cost × 100 = ($180,000 − $80,000) ÷ $80,000 × 100 = $100,000 ÷ $80,000 × 100 = 125%. BCR = Total Benefits ÷ Programme Cost = $180,000 ÷ $80,000 = 2.25. Interpretation: BCR of 2.25 means every $1 invested returned $2.25 in gross benefits. ROI of 125% means for every $1 invested, the programme returned $1.25 in NET profit (after recovering the investment cost). Both are positive indicators. Option A reverses the formulas — a common exam error.
§III · Management Theories
Management Theories — Overview

BoK III.A.2 explicitly names six categories of management theory the exam tests: scientific, organizational, behavioral, learning, systems thinking, and situational/complexity. You must know each theory's core premise, its era, its limitation, and how it connects to quality management.

📚 BoK: III.A.2
⚠️ Note: These theories build on each other chronologically — each emerged as a critique of the previous
1
The Chronological Evolution
EraTheoryCore premiseKey limitation
1900s–1920sScientific ManagementFind the one best way; separate thinking from doing; maximize efficiencyTreats people as machines; ignores human motivation and satisfaction
1910s–1930sClassical Organizational TheoryStudy management of the larger enterprise; principles of coordination, hierarchy, division of laborStill mechanical; misses human dynamics at organizational scale
1930s–1950sBehavioral TheoryHuman relations matter; motivation, attitudes, and group dynamics affect performanceCan over-emphasize social factors; underestimates technical and structural requirements
1950s–presentLearning TheoriesBehavior is shaped by antecedents and consequences (A-B-C); reinforce desired behaviorsRisk of manipulation; ignores intrinsic motivation if applied crudely
1990s–presentSystems ThinkingOrganizations are interconnected systems; parts cannot be understood in isolation; mental models shape actionComplex to implement; requires significant cultural and leadership commitment
2000s–presentComplexity TheoryOrganizations are complex adaptive systems; they self-organize; cannot be fully controlled by top-down managementStill emerging; not always actionable for day-to-day management decisions
2
The Exam Test Pattern
💡 How the exam tests management theories
The exam presents a management scenario and asks which theory best explains it, or presents a theory and asks what management approach it recommends. The key is knowing the CORE PREMISE and the QUALITY MANAGEMENT CONNECTION for each theory — not deep philosophical details.
§III · Topic 10
Scientific Management & Classical Organizational Theory
📚 BoK: III.A.2
1
Scientific Management (Taylor, Gilbreth, Gantt)

Frederick Taylor was the first major contributor to scientific management theory. His core principle: find the ONE BEST WAY to perform any task by applying systematic observation, measurement, and experimentation. Key features:

ContributorKey contributionQuality relevance
Frederick TaylorTime and motion studies; separating planning (managers/engineers) from execution (workers); standard methods for every taskFoundation of work standardization — the same principle drives SOPs, standard work, and ISO 9001's documented process requirements
Frank & Lillian GilbrethMotion study — analyzing every physical motion in a task to eliminate waste; therblig analysisDirectly precedes lean manufacturing's waste elimination philosophy; process optimization through systematic motion analysis
Henry GanttGantt chart for project scheduling; incentive pay systems based on outputGantt chart remains a standard quality improvement project management tool today
⚠️ Taylor's critical limitation — and why it matters for quality culture
Taylor assumed workers were motivated primarily by money and needed to be told exactly what to do. He separated thinking (engineers) from doing (workers). This produced efficiency gains but also created the disengaged workforce that quality professionals like Deming later had to rehabilitate. Deming's Point 9 (Break down barriers between departments) and Point 12 (Remove barriers to pride of workmanship) are direct responses to Taylor's over-divided labor model.
2
Classical Organizational Theory

As organizations grew larger and more complex in the early 20th century, the study of management expanded from individual task optimization to managing the entire enterprise. Key concepts:

ConceptDescriptionQuality connection
Division of laborSpecialization of roles for efficiency — people become expert at their specific functionQuality becomes a specialized function — but creates the "that's not my job" silo mentality quality managers must overcome
Scalar chain (hierarchy)Clear chain of authority from top to bottom; every employee reports to one superiorFormal authority structure defines the quality manager's legitimate power — and its limits in cross-functional work
Unity of commandEach person reports to exactly one manager — no dual reportingDirectly conflicts with matrix organizational structures quality improvement teams often use
Span of controlA manager can effectively supervise only a limited number of peopleDetermines how many quality engineers a quality manager can effectively develop and oversee
💡 Classical theory's legacy in quality systems
